notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0224b.stoa001.opp-l: Prologue: the addressee is Bishop Perpetuus of Tours, with a play on 'perpetuus' ('perpetual'); the 'history' sent is presumably Sulpicius Severus' Life of Martin. In pr.2, the subject of 'ignoscat', 'ferat', 'irascatur' is unexpressed (probably Martin, or 'clementia'); the sentence 'ferat murmura ... fortiori' is obscure. 1.17–18: the edition's full stop after 'sacram' seems misplaced; 'sacram ... legem' read together. 1.66: stray mark omitted; 'erumna' = aerumna; 'linguae partes' is obscure. 1.95: stray line number omitted. 1.114: 'ope\'' read as 'ope'. 1.124: 'nonum' read as 'nouum' (new). 1.76–78: the sense of the doubled cloak passage is uncertain. 1.126: two years short of four lustra = eighteen years.

Lines 152–165, 219–226: opening quotation marks are printed as \' in the source; treated as ordinary quotation marks. Line 342 opens a quotation with no evident speaker; this may be an editorial misplacement, or the beginning of the revived man's (or the poet's) exclamation; translated as given. Line 343 'in primo mundo' is obscure ('in the first [view of the] world', i.e. on first returning to life). Stray marks ('•' at 214, '<' at 224, the full stop after 'rura' at 251, '320' at 320) and the comma after 'penetralia' at 210 are taken as scanning artefacts. Line 177 'uiolares' (second person) sits awkwardly beside 'adficerent' (third person) in 178; translated as given. Line 189 'inferiora moenia' (lower ramparts), i.e. a lower office, is figurative. Line 233–235: the mother 'born to God' through her son refers to baptism ('lauacro'). Line 300 'clamaret ... Foebum' could also mean 'would call Phoebus wretched'.

1.355-356: 'renewed by the eternal wave' refers to baptism. 2.13 'cathedrae': the bishop's chair, i.e. his episcopate. 2.33: stray '1' read as a footnote mark. 2.63/2.78: wordplay on the name Defensor and 'defensorem' in the psalm verse (Ps. 8:3), which is quoted in a form adapted to the name. 2.105: 'holy wood' is likely the Cross. 2.122: 'ordine' (the right hand by order) is uncertain in sense, perhaps the orderly forming of letters. 2.125-126: the construction is awkward, and the translation is approximate. 2.140: 'odor' (scent) may stand for the strength or flavour of the wine.

Line 2.231 begins with an opening quotation mark in the text that has no evident speech; it appears to be a stray mark and is ignored. Line 2.303 ('praecessit celeres properantia uota furores') is obscure; rendered literally, it seems to mean the pagans' eager hopes ran ahead of the tree's swift fall. In 2.276 'subiectis subditus' is difficult; the rendering is tentative.

362: Leprosus is taken as the name of the village (Levroux, as in Sulpicius Severus). 391 is placed by the edition between 393 and 392's sequence as given; translated in the order supplied. 441–442: 'surgit... in ensem' rendered literally ('rises to the sword'), i.e. rears up to strike. 466: a stray '\'' after 'uoluntas' is a scanning artefact and has been ignored. 541: a stray initial full stop has been ignored.

2.571: 'gratantur uterque' (plural verb with uterque) taken as 'both give thanks'; stray comma omitted. 2.595: 'dilato uulnere' read as 'the wound deferred/held off'; sense uncertain. 2.676: 'stomacho' taken as the girl's chest. 2.692–702: Paulinus is Paulinus of Nola; the author plays on his own shared name. 3.14–15: Maximus's victims are Gratian (killed) and Valentinian II (exiled).

Line 3.75: simma = sigma, the semicircular dining couch. Lines 3.119–120 are obscure and probably corrupt ('ulli' perhaps for 'nulli'); the sense seems to be that Martin barely touched the wine with his lips; translation tentative. Line 3.134: punctuation and syntax unclear ('praesentem uincere mundum' stands without a governing verb); rendered literally. Line 3.142: Maximus' first victory and later capture by Theodosius are meant. Line 3.214–215: Juno, sister and wife of Jupiter.

Lines 246-253 continue Martin's address to the devil. Line 250: 'omnibus et qui' leaves the clause incomplete before the gap. Line 251 is corrupt in the edition ('per ........ mixtus culpis. merito. admiscere. poenis.'); only fragments are translated, and the syntax cannot be recovered. Line 311: 'tenebris ei;' is evidently a misreading, probably for 'tenebrisque'; translated as 'in the darkness'. Line 295: 'graucm' read as 'grauem'. Line 363: '0' read as 'O'. Line 412: 'cui ... cohaeres' is understood to refer to God.

3.454-458: the martyr is Stephen (Acts 7). 4.21 onward: the scanned text has stray punctuation (4.23, 4.27, 4.69, 4.186), ignored; 4.60 '11011' read as 'non'. 4.85: sense of 'nec dubia hoc uotum mox coniectura probauit' uncertain; perhaps 'no doubtful inference soon showed [God] approved this wish'. 4.163: the line seems defective or a line has dropped (infinitive 'prodere' without governing verb); rendered as continuing the purpose clause. 4.180-182: Balaam's ass (Num. 22); the Latin compresses the construction. 4.193-194: 'solo de lumine Christi ... pensant tenebras' is obscure; perhaps 'make up for the darkness with the light of Christ alone'.

Line 4.396 stands in the edition's order between 4.393 and 4.394; it is translated in the position given, where it continues the comparison with the Queen of Sheba. Line 242 is elliptical (conferte ... titulos pompasque iubentum); the comparison with Martin's miracles is implied, and 'with miracles' is supplied. In 4.244 'regi' probably refers to the Lord as king, as against 'your king' (vestri regis) in 4.239; the sense is uncertain. In 4.246 'sacerdos' (Martin) is addressed as the poet's Muse. 4.361-362 lacks a main verb ('congaudens ... pandere'); 'was glad' is supplied. In 4.369-370 'remotis ... ministris' is taken as 'the servants removed'. 'ah alto' (4.326) is read as 'ab alto'.

Lines 401–403 address the empress (wife of Maximus) from the preceding episode. Line 508–509: the image of riders leaning so far forward that they seem to outrun their horses is compressed; rendered literally. Line 539–540: 'at quam' read as exclamatory.

4.641: 'leporem' (charm, grace) is odd here; it seems to refer to the man's teachable yielding, and the sense is uncertain. 4.643: 'floren' is evidently corrupt (perhaps for 'florentes' or 'florem'); rendered as 'flourishing'. 4.629: 'contiguo sudore' is obscure; rendered 'in close-pressed sweat'. 5.12: wordplay on 'rea supplicii' (liable to punishment) and 'rea uoti' (bound to fulfil a vow). 5.106-112: the English lines are slightly rearranged across breaks for word order.

Lines 157 and 160: the subject of the colour change and 'pinguido' (presumably for pinguedo/pinguitudine, 'richness') are uncertain. Line 167: stray full stop after 'iustum' ignored. Line 256: '(\'t' read as 'et'. Line 270: 'motam;' read as 'motant'. Lines 307-308: the construction 'idem quod fautor sceleris, qui criminis ultor' is compressed; rendered as the judge, avenger of crime, becoming guilty himself. Line 195: Severus is Sulpicius Severus (Chronicle in two books; Life of Martin). Line 271: Phalaris, the tyrant of Acragas, applied as a byname to Avitianus.

5.381: 'parci cupis: esto remissus' is compressed; taken as 'you wish [them] to be spared: let [it] be remitted', though the masculine 'remissus' is awkward and the text may be corrupt. 5.428: 'reus' and 'tortor' appear to describe the possessed person and the tormenting demon as one hanging figure; the sense is uncertain. Scanning errors silently corrected (e.g. 'pendeutia' for 'pendentia').

Line 528 onward: 'Ambatia' is Amboise. Line 544: 'geniumque dei de nomine fabri' is obscure; it seems to mean the god was named after (or identified with) the builder. Line 573: a stray full stop after 'molis,' has been ignored. Line 650: 'iussarum ... aquarum' is taken loosely as 'the waters as ordered'. Line 676: 'esocem' (esox) is rendered 'pike'; the identification of the fish is uncertain. Line 683: a stray full stop after 'adplaudens' has been ignored. Line 717: 'Ithacianam' refers to the party of Ithacius, the opponent of Priscillian.

5.733 'praesentis' taken as genitive: 'one present' (i.e. Martin in person). 5.796 'quis' read as 'quibus' (by which). 5.826 the punctuation 'iam laeso iudice' is taken as an ablative absolute qualifying the hard case. 5.835 'quam' read as 'quam[diu]/donec' ('until'), continuing 'nec prius absistit'. 5.853–856 obscure: the money, refused for himself, was spent on ransoming captives; 'numerata fidem, contempta rigorem' is rendered literally. 6.1 'murmura' presumably means the poet's verses. 6.25–28 the 'interpres' is evidently Sulpicius Severus, Martin's biographer. 6.45 the syntax is elliptical: 'sentitur' probably applies to both nouns. 5.777 and 5.853 contain stray punctuation, which has been ignored.

6.113–144: the besieged city is evidently Arles (bridge of boats over the Rhône), with Aegidius as commander. 6.148 'specularia' (lit. windows/look-outs) is obscure; rendered 'prospect'. 6.158 'omnibus inuitat trepidos' is obscure; sense uncertain. 6.92 and 6.95: the plural 'mentes' and shift to singular are as in the text. 6.203 'tyrauni' read as 'tyranni'. Stray dots in 6.96 and 6.244 omitted.

263: the stray 'em' after 'timorem' is taken as a scanning error or footnote mark and omitted. 317: 'inspecta Siloa' is obscure; rendered as a comparison with Siloam, but the construction is uncertain. 333–334: the 'sowing' apparently refers to the wax buried in the field; the sense is uncertain. 368: 'alterna fides' is unclear; rendered 'mutual faith'. 411: 'com minus' read as 'comminus'. 424–425: the punctuation of the edition is odd; 'obsidione maris' is taken with the preceding clause.
Line 504 is obscure; 'praeconia' may refer to the proclamation of the miracles themselves as opposed to the poet's verse.

nodes.text: I. Six Books on the Life of Saint Martin the Bishop. Prologue.
To his holy and most blessed lord, his special patron before God, venerable with all reverence and admiration, and truly apostolic teacher in all religion, Bishop Perpetuus: Paulinus.

In your zeal of charity and your warmth of affection you bid me forget my modesty, though you urge modesty and reserve, lest judgement be weighed down by transgression. You do not see that you are deceived, judging more kindly than truly: you believe good what you wish to be good, and you admit into the fellowship of your devotion even those whom you have chosen from among the foolish. You sent me so splendid a history of the merits and miracles of our holy and apostolic teacher and lord that it would most rightly come to the knowledge of the whole world, had your blessing so ordered. But you judged that I could keep to these footsteps and add something, as if more polished, though it is a far greater thing to bring out what has been discovered than to copy out what has already been published. Let me consent nevertheless to submit in obedience, and not weigh my own awareness of my limits too rashly, since I think one ought not to question what he commands to whom the wish to obey submits itself in all things. Holy and most blessed lord, truly patron of perpetual religion and grace, mirror of venerable teaching, model of perfection: follow him whom you love, imitate him whom you follow, his successor in honour, his venerator in humility.

Let me hold to the terms of your command. Take for yourself what is yours, you who, as you know, made me answerable by this choice. When the paper comes into your hands, cherish what you receive, excuse my lack of skill, entreat clemency: may he pardon the presumption, help the one who errs, come to the aid of the mistake. It was unworthy that I should dare to touch deeds so great, but it would have been more arrogant to despise your commands. May he bear with patience the murmurs he received through grace, and not be angry at a boldness made stronger by joy. Our God wishes the things he deigns to work through him to be made known, whoever proclaims them. Cherish with your patronage the one you took up, unknown, through those treasures of charity.
Book One.
Christ had spread a venerable light through all the world,
unlocking the mysteries of the kingdom of the Gospel.
But since the working of miracles had not moved all nations,
and with frail understanding they hesitated to believe
whatever a messenger had published from foreign shores
(for things learned move by words, things present by facts:
the unseen is urged on us, but the seen is proved),
therefore he, whose mercy is equal toward the whole world,
sowed very many miracles in our lands too,
giving to the furthest Gauls the glories of Martin.
Fruitful Pannonia sent him from far away for our salvation,
born of no lowly stock, but of a tribune.
For his father was famed with praise for his merits; but this man
was nobler than such famous forebears, who, with Christ as father,
spurned sacrilegious rites, well degenerate from his father.
For scarcely in his tenth year, already older in his ways,
he passed over to the sacred law; with steadfast heart
he signed his holy brow with the protection of the cross.
His mind was not unsteady in his tender breast: his whole
will was to keep God's command and to know it,
to shun the gatherings of men, to know the secret places
of the blessed desert, and, spurning the world, to know God,
to leave earthly cares behind with lofty heart.
When he was attempting this at scarcely twice six years,
the lofty glory of so great a deed was shut off from him,
but God counted it as merit, who approved the will.
The Augustus commands that, in a levy to prepare for war,
all the offspring of veteran stock be equipped.
What will envy not do? His father betrays him and thrusts
arms on his son. Alas, fatherly love forgetful of so great a danger!
Rather, if your stony mind admits any feeling,
grow great through your [son's] honours: for it is more your praise to be surpassed.
Only look at all he has done with holy vow:
if they are good, imitate them gladly; if hard, rejoice.
The soldier of Christ is put in chains as a soldier of the world,
but the mind is not dragged along, nor is the heart bound with the flesh.
The names of recruitment are empty: he has long been a soldier,
who, taken by his own king, through very many battles
conquered avarice and overthrew proud
luxury: ambition lies already laid low
by his strength, and fury and anger flee his firm mind,
and deadly pride, which outdoes all faults.
Setting out, he scarcely allows one companion to go with him,
a servant bound not by labour, but only in name.
O happy man, for whom so pleasing a condition prepared
such a yoke that the rival wishes of noble men
might contend with you for your lot,
if only they might serve. But you too, freed from the law
of your birth, are driven under a hard law:
for the devotion of the saint, made subject, serves you.
The same clothing, the shared fare of a sparing table,
he first in services, so that no cleverness at all
could tell that the servant was preferred to the master.
Now, what grace he had with his equals, and how modestly
true love had made even his seniors submit to him;
then how great his strictness in the food he took,
lest a stuffed belly should spoil his quick perception
or the burden of the limbs weigh down his watchful mind,
so that his supply, divided, might give a part to the needy,
and what would overwhelm one might better refresh both.
For he had so divided everything among the needy who begged
that only coverings were left for his wasted limbs:
when suddenly, in winter bristling with icy cold,
a naked man hurries to meet him, shivering, scarcely uttering
words, halving them, broken in their sound; but his plight
frees his speech, and his distress cries out the parts his tongue [could not].
All pass by, and the madness of the rich
scorned his loathed complaint with wretched laughter.
The saint stood still, uncertain, troubled in heart,
what to do: for the wish was there, the means were not.
If he covered him, he must be stripped. Yet not even so did
any delay of hesitation hold back the glorious deed.
Only one thing had remained to cover his blessed body:
as always, a doubled cloak, which kept off cold and rain
and the rage of the winds with its twofold wrapping.
For the hanging part makes up for the part cut away
if the body, warmed by the added wool, feels that what
would have been lacking to the head has gone to increase the warmth.
But the blessed judgement of his strict vow
rejects this and condemns it as a loss to the heart,
that the caution of a timid faith should thus have preferred
to grant to one person's limbs the part added by the doubled covering
rather than divide it between two.
No delay slows the work, but his right hand outstrips his wish:
the deed accomplished whatever his mind saw must be done.
The unconquered sword is drawn, guiltless of a wound,
and lavish mercy cuts the cloak through the middle,
choosing, I believe, the worse half for himself. Then the limbs of the trembling man
he covers, and, giving some warmth from his garment,
now with lighter clothing takes on himself part of the cold.
O happy man, by your virtue surpassing
all miracles and exceeding the precepts of the Lord who commands!
For he bids us be content with little
and not to keep two garments: you divide your one.
All look on. Some laugh at the unsightly
covering, and do not see the truer beauty in his heart.
But others, with stricken heart, lament to themselves
that the righteousness of a poor man could decide for the needy
what ample substance with its rich wealth had refused.
Nor is there delay before the palm is rendered for so great a triumph.
For scarcely had he thrown his weary limbs on his bed,
admitting a light sleep, but with a watchful heart
(nor was that sleep, for his attentive mind stayed vigorous),
when suddenly before his eyes, kindly with a generous reward,
Christ stood, clothed in his own poor man,
and fitted the blessed covering to his own limbs.
O truly precious cloak! What such thing have splendid garments earned,
whether of purple or of gold drawn into thread
from gleaming skeins? What of silks, smooth
to the touch, or lifelike with skilfully worked figures?
He, God of men and earth, of sea and sky,
who gave all things, without whom is nothing, to whom belong
the very things we gave, and we who gave, both gift and giver,
is enriched by this wealth, if he counts the gains of salvation.
Yet not even from this did boasting shake
his steady mind, nor did he feel vain swelling in his heart.
O virtue near to God, to count nothing to one's praise
when you do praiseworthy things, and not to ascribe to our own doing
what we do, and to have God praised in every act!
Now surely he was secure about so great a judge,
but he is not puffed up even by fellowship with Christ:
the things seen increase his faith; renewed by the holy washing,
his limbs shine and take on beauty equal to his heart,
and the mysteries of the font bring forth a new body.
And yet, shining with this maturity of character and flesh,
he had lived two years short of four lustra,
I believe because the Holy Spirit had first enriched
his whole heart with the stream of a watering gift:
as once holy Peter saw blessed gifts
sent ahead by the Lord in such a soldier.
Who, I ask, though good, will be able to finish thus
as blessed Martin began in his tender years?
And yet, doing these things, he did not think he had even begun,
because he had delayed a little, scarcely two years,
already a monk in merit, but a soldier in name only,
to break off the empty titles of a world already trampled,
waiting for the holy fellowship of the tribune who promised it,
so that, with Christ soon as judge, salvation doubled through the vows
of two might make up for a small and just delay.
Meanwhile, the barriers broken and the frontier burst through,
a fierce enemy had begun to lay waste the Gallic countryside.
The emperor prepares to go to meet him, and all the companies,
summoned by command, exhortation, entreaty, and largess,
he musters for war. For those whom fear holds back,
rewards entice, and gifts conquer fear.
But a mind full of God fears nothing, scorns all things,
laughs at terror, and tramples earthly rewards.
So when those ahead, going first, had taken the gift,
as the order ran its course, the saint is called in the usual way.
he spurns the present gifts of the pressing king,
and with these words he goes against the tyrant's words:
'Hand to another, prince, these earthly gifts, this money:
greater rewards of a greater king await me.
This is the wage of war: let those who wish to fight take it.'
At these words, then, the prince is inflamed to savage anger,
charging that, a coward at the time of war,
unmindful of glory, he had invented pretexts for his fear.
But he [replied]: 'I have no dread of the pressing danger,
nor do steadfast hearts fear an easy death.
In short, what words set out, deeds too will prove.
I first, going ahead of the columns with weapons thrown aside,
seizing not the arms of man but the signs of salvation,
trusting not in the cover of a shield but in the name of Christ,
and setting the cross on my brow as a help in place of a helmet,
will meet all dangers with a fearless heart.'
He assented, and so that proofs might confirm the truth of the saying,
the pious man is ordered to be held in harsh custody.
And now the newly risen day was sprinkling the earth
with its first light: a suppliant embassy comes to the king,
bowing submissive necks to the dominion of the one who commands.
What, I ask, do we see achieved here by men, what by arms?
What did the iron-clad battle line avail, what terror and sword?
What wedge fell to javelins, what squadron to arrows?
One man, and trust in the eternal king alone,
conquered countless peoples without the wound of slaughter.
Here, Martin, is your triumph, with Christ fighting,
so that you would not at least defile your holy face with blood,
nor the deaths of the dying afflict your pious mind.
So, eager by merit and keener from success itself,
with his enemies crushed he hastens to conquer the world.
He seeks out Hilary, a teacher of the faith proved
by so many evidences. Lest boastfulness inflict any wound
or his own heart's opinion exalt him,
though already a teacher he acts the disciple, and is proved greater
while he desires to be lesser: for to despise praise is praise.
So too, though already worthy of the honour of the chief chair,
he refuses it, so that he might at least be distinguished with the honour of deacon,
and he scarcely accepted a place he had long surpassed in holy conduct,
asking for lower ramparts for himself:
an exorcist in rank, but already a priest in virtue.
Then, lest earthly piety should at least find fault
with one whom divine piety so particularly guided,
he wishes with eager desire to visit the authors of his birth
and to turn their averted minds to better things.
For a headlong and straying error oppressed his father and mother,
who worshipped sacrilegious rites and stones or bronzes,
with an all-too-powerful death while they were living.
So, when he had set out on the road, piety went as his companion, and
an angel sent by the Lord had paved all the regions,
so that a gentle ascent might lie open, the hill being lowered,
and steep places and hollows might not drag him into headlong falls.
And while he was quickly crossing the cloud-bearing Alps,
caught by chance in an ambush of savage robbers,
[facing] threatening swords, with his hands bound behind his back,
he laughed, and with unmoved face despised the danger.
Indeed, to recall the wonders of so great a deed,
he is said to have saved his guard with counsels of salvation,
this one a truer guard of the soul than that one of the body.
For the one did not even have [Martin's] limbs under his control,
while the other bound the inmost recesses of the averted mind.
But yet both skilfully taught the way to be followed:
this one showed the way of the road, and learned that of salvation.
So he completes the journey he had begun and draws near his homeland,
having entered the fields of Hesperia after crossing the Alps.
Here again the enemy of his constant holy endeavours,
feigning human appearance with a counterfeit body,
presented himself, coming to meet him, and dared to
ask him where he was heading and what this haste required.
He [replied] to this: 'Christ is my only way and guide: in him
is the fulfilment of the purpose, by whom the will was given.'
But that demon, gnashing his teeth, went against him with all his efforts,
meeting him, offended at so great an undertaking.
To him the saint [said]: 'The Lord defends, the enemy does not harm:
with God as helper no opposing power can
be feared. Fearing the Lord, I despise danger.
That fear makes me not fear.' After he had spoken
such things, the shade was driven off and vanished from his eyes.
And when, with the Lord as guide, he reached his parents' presence,
and since perdition, hardened, with habit persuading it, held
his father, who refused the words of salvation pressed on him,
he at least then won back his mother, by Christ's gift.
O happy in so great a birth, she who bore a son
through whom she was born to God, and by one childbirth was made
both mother and infant! The mother who was to be begotten
first bore from her womb the one through whom she has now arisen in the blessed bath.
Yet many more yielded to the saving example,
rightly marvelling at the marks of such great character.
And at that time, as it happened, the evil error of a deadly doctrine
had spread among the peoples, followers of incautious heart,
the poison which Arius had poured from his insane mouth.
But above all this plague held Illyricum infected,
having raged through it deeply with all its venom.
Here, while he, strong in steadfast virtue, dares to strive against it,
and while he breaks the waves with his opposing breast,
while he often rebukes priests, often the people,
overwhelmed by the plots of all, having suffered beatings,
driven out at last, he left his earthly dwelling:
yet he kept the faith on his lips and salvation in his heart.
So when he judged that he must yield, lest the madness of an overturned world
should overwhelm the saint if he lingered,
he seeks the Gallic countryside again, and retraces
the steps he had noted, not unmindful of the faith.
But since the deadly error was raging over the whole world,
and these crimes were pressing even the remotest Gauls,
and since the faction of an insane world had thrust out
Hilary himself, the wall of the faith and its strong column,
he decided to rest a little in a cell he had built
here, where most beautiful Milan adorns Italy,
which rejoices in the shade of grove and vine.
From here too he goes away driven out, leaving lands and walls
and seeking the sea and its waves, because the water was more trustworthy
as a lodging, and the storm of the people and the mob was more
to be feared than that of the sea. A priest of the same merit
and like danger accompanies him as he goes.
An island is chosen as a lodging, far from any host.
Grass is enough for food. Using its roots,
the saints double their fasts with so barren a diet.
And while without discrimination they search out for meagre food
whatever the bowels of the untried earth offered,
they suddenly felt the plant of hellebore with its venom
spreading a deadly poison through all their limbs.
They go to the Lord with all the power of praying,
but his mercy went ahead of their prayers. Nothing was done by arts,
but a present medicine was the only hope of health.
Let us consider, we who are accustomed to seek life with our whole fortune,
poured out on doctors as the wage of their fee,
so that our time of living may grow through our money,
what potions of choice juices achieved here,
and remedies once gathered from ancient books.
Here surely the heart earned swift health without cost or art,
and the word gave it: let us marvel and rejoice.
The voice is silent, and the case is made by the cry of the silent.
The physician is felt and not seen: all the limbs,
their pores closed, admit the whole cure into their inward parts.
Meanwhile it is reported that at last, from unjust exile,
the holy bishop is returning by the king's orders,
with whom he had shared the fellowship of an illustrious life,
while the teacher was flourishing in the region of the Pictavi,
delivering the precepts of salvation to untamed peoples.
And although piety, swift in affection, had hurried the rejoicing saint
quickly away, still that man, impatient
of delay, had already left the lofty walls
of high Rome, to be carried back more quickly to the Pictonian region.
So, following the steps that went before him on a pious course,
he earned his heart's desire and the end of his labour.
Here he builds a cell, a solace for weary limbs:
for his mind, full of God, remained in the heavenly seat.
Here, if only we were to recall the songs of the ancient bards,
when wonders suddenly shook their astonished senses,
mindless madness would cry out to wretched Phoebus,
and would not let the false Muses rest even a little;
the Delphic temples would be shaken by a lying Apollo,
and the whole crowd of the deaf sisters would be swept along,
or roused monsters would fill out the whole frenzy:
we, whose understanding and words are sought from Christ,
pray that you, Martin, worshipper of Christ, inspire us a little.
You, who were able to give back life to the dead,
upheld by the Lord's help, give back health to me:
I first will perform the miracle of life granted,
I first will burst the bars of the stinking tomb.
Dead with my whole heart, I pray a just prayer to my patron,
that a living mind may speak the titles of such great praise.
So, although the lofty deeds overcome the powers of speech,
and the measure of eloquence cannot match his praises,
I will make the attempt. You, whoever, reading, despise such worthless
verses, while you mock the words, will marvel at the deeds.
A certain man, seeing the wonders of so famous a life,
chose to join himself to so great a master,
one whom the mystic water of the font had not yet renewed.
A fever, feeding deep through all his marrow,
wrenched out his slender life, his body consumed.
And at that time, as it happened, the teacher was absent: but the attentive
devotion of the brothers was sorrowfully lamenting the lifeless corpse,
grieving at the punishment of a brother, not the death of the flesh.
Arriving, the saint bathes his face with abundant weeping,
pitying the sad fate of the dead man, and filled
the whole place with his cries. Soon, with witnesses removed,
he burst into the cell, made sorrowful by so sad a death.
Then he threw himself upon his lifeless friend,
embraces the cold limbs with all his limbs,
breathing a faint breath over the rigid face.
Yet his whole hope is referred entirely to the Lord:
the accustomed mercy is prayed to, the known compassion
is asked for, and by believing he earns the merit of faith.
The confidence of a pure heart saw God present,
and the inward parts felt the effect of the holy breaths.
Without delay, the prayer is scarcely held in suspense for two hours:
little by little the linen cloths move as the limbs stir,
and the dry limbs are moistened with the fluid of the veins,
and with the breath of the soul the icy breast grows warm,
the clouded eyes are unsealed with light poured in,
'Happy those to whom, at the rising of the light granted them,
it befell to see Martin in the first [view of the] world.
the whole body rises with a sudden effort,
and the skin, long since sallow on the wasted limbs,
takes back a crimson flush with healthier sap.
His voice is easy, his step firm, his hand capable, his heart strong:
the whole man, from a body made up of various elements,
received a single life in its different functions.
Soon the greatest joy draws out a great cry:
his tongue sounds praises, messengers of a thankful mind,
the shout of his mouth proclaims the feeling of his heart.
Soon the crowd burst through the doors and filled the cell,
and a harmonious chorus sang the holy man's praises.
But he, so as to renew his life completely after death,
at once shone, renewed by the eternal wave,
and, fortunate, drew out his old age over many years,
for no short time a witness of so glorious a deed.
For he used often to tell many people
that he had trembled before the tribunal of the eternal Judge,
consigned to vile throngs and plunged in darkness,
until a prayer, brought forward in the words of angels,
offered his vow to the Lord and brought back his life.
He was the first to make Martin known to our shores;
by this entrance his glory came to its further praises.
Indeed not much time had flowed by after these miracles:
a new glory hastens on a famous deed.
For while he was passing by the neighbouring estate of Lupicinus,
no lowly or insignificant man, but a man known almost through the world
for his excellence, so that thereby the more brightly
the glory confirmed by so great a witness might be plain,
drawing the unlearned people on through so many miracles,
hearing from afar the pitiful cries of people weeping,
he stopped: he asks the cause and learns in turn,
and just compassion stirred his pious grief.
For one servant, with a noose tightening on his throat,
had madly burst the bounds of life wrenched from him.
He runs up quickly and embraces the sad corpse,
the eyes forced out and the throat drained of blood,
the eyes too grim, and the face menacing in death.
Again weeping to the Lord, again sighs
and groans, the cry of the heart, the loud voice of one silent:
the same faith of merit, and no unequal grace of the gift.
He is received by a thankful chorus, with a crowd pressing round:
they display to all the miracles of Christ the Lord
and the spoil taken from the enemy, the joy of the believing people.
BOOK TWO.
See, a new sea opens, and kindly breezes
have drawn the leaky keel into the midst of the waves,
and while the joys of the calmed sea carry me away,
my rash skiff has burst into the vast deep,
barely grazing the shores even of the nearby lands.
Now what do I do, and where in fear do I steer my wavering prow?
The winds urge on the course; fear urges return.
Let us press on, since land is far off, where the wave will draw us:
only may Martin's spirit spread
a calm breeze and so grant a light wind to the traveller
that the rotten sail may bear the fortunate gusts.
Up to now, in recounting the monk's ways and deeds,
there was shore: now the sea will be the teaching of the bishop's chair.
Now I shall unfold the famous deeds of the great bishop.
Once there flourished greatly in the lands of the Gauls
the city of the Turones, wide in fields and full of people.
But, desiring to be stronger still with such a bishop,
it burned with all its prayers to win Martin for itself.
But, driving pride wholly from his holy heart,
his humble mind remained unmoved by frequent pleas,
until, by contrived words and forced tears,
righteous lies overcame his excessive firmness.
For a certain man, aware of his great compassion, begs him,
pitying the sad trouble of his sick wife,
to deign to visit with holy prayer one who asked it:
he would be either the cause of her recovery by coming quickly,
or of her death, if harsh resolve delayed his prayers.
Sighs too are joined to the feigned words,
and sobbing cries with broken murmur.
He kisses his knees, clasps his feet in his arms,
surpassing true grief through so many fictions.
What wonder if a simple spirit, a holy mind, follows one who calls him,
when God compels? For he himself would rather
have exposed the deceitful device, did he not approve what was to be done.
As he went out, a crowd of people receives him, doing
kindly violence, and a numerous uprising of petitioners
throngs the road, a peaceful commotion, a tumult without bitterness,
and an all-night guard even posts watchful
sentries and guards its master, who was to be guarded.
Harmonious joys exult with equal prayers.
They go out to meet him; from all the gates there rushes towards him
eagerness and the people's vying favour: one will
for all, and no division of mind in their zeal.
Some, devouring envy infects with the gall
of black poison, and, burning the hearts of the wretches with its goads,
a fleshly opinion draws them back to the opposing side.
They say too, which it is a sin to believe, that some
bishops of learned mind had caught a like madness,
mocking things that they should have rejoiced in: that no grace
had adorned his venerable face, that, with his hair cut off,
his uncovered brow displayed the whole sign of the Lord,
and did not weigh on his eyes with a cloud of quivering locks,
that his shabby clothing, attesting the brightness of his heart,
betrayed his zeal in prayer, because often, when his limbs
were rolled on the ground with body prostrate, the dust pressed in
had stuck, rough, in the dirty wool.
Rightly, then, so perverse a will gave way to the people,
and the sounder judgement of the common folk overcame the leading men.
For truly no one could fail to know the judgement
of Christ who called him, proved by so many signs.
For of the rest, whom a fierce faction, wanting the contrary,
had wrongfully allied to itself, the one more violent
was a bishop, Defensor: by that name they thought
perhaps that the efforts of their false plan
would be defended, though God refused, who approved what was just.
For the pious people were celebrating the customary rite in holy assembly,
viewing the mysteries in a crowded gathering,
while the dense throngs pressed closer round the altars
and the supporters hung in great numbers on their own wishes,
and the reader could not pass the obstacles in his way.
But a deacon who happened to be there, barely snatching the book,
seized hastily the verse which the page of the psalm, opened
at once, first presented,
on the spur of the moment, singing these words of the ancient prophet:
'Out of the mouth of infants, and from the little murmur
of sucklings, you have made tender tongues unfold praise
because of your enemies, so that this praise, brought forth
by little ones, may destroy the perverse defender.'
A shout is raised to heaven, and the judgement is proved
present, with God crying out: the sentence of Christ
overwhelmed the opposing side with a thunderbolt of words.
For the same verse approved the wishes of those who praised
and checked the envious hearts of those who resisted.
Nor was the monk's labour any less after that, because his glory grew
by right of the bishop's office. What should be done is taught by deeds:
the work of example persuades more than the grace of speech.
So he kept his cheapest clothing with its worn covering,
so the precious modesty of his humble, holy heart,
so the happy resolve of his unremitting life remains.
At first, then, his cell was joined
to the holy altars. Soon, so that his secluded prayer
might avoid the thronging people and the constant crowds,
he went out and withdrew two miles from the city.
Nor did so great a nearness harm the remote cell:
a secret lodging for the monk, a short way for the teacher,
a near house for the instructor, a distant one for the man at leisure.
On one side, with the edge of a naturally sheer rock,
a curving cliff had enclosed it in a small recess;
on the other the Loire, with its banks bent in a slight curve,
had hedged in the enclosed ground with its stream stretched before it,
and one narrow entrance lay open between the cliff and the river,
where, separated a little by a confined path,
the river's flow touches the edges of the hill.
Here he preferred to put together a small cell from a pile of timber,
recognising the mysteries of the holy wood,
a most exalted guest entering under a humble roof,
so that the modesty of the brothers gathered there, thus taught,
might learn to despise pomp at little cost,
eagerly imitating the master who went before them in examples.
But others did not like timber, and in the hollowed hill
the nearby cliff offers dug-out recesses.
Just admiration had drawn eighty brothers there
to the mirror of such excellence, so that from it
a happy imitation might take the ways it observed.
No one had anything of his own; all things were common
to all: love drew on a shared stock.
No one was granted the right to sell anything,
lest the wicked hunger for gold, once tasted, should grow.
He forbids the practice of a trade. One pursuit
is allowed, that of writing, which occupies mind and eyes and hands
and holds them all at once in one point,
the gaze by sight, the heart by its senses, the right hand by order.
Yet only the younger age is kept to these things.
For the mind already mature has enough in prayer,
so that, one whose understanding a senior judgement confirms
should strive for purity of heart and keep watch to cleanse
the hidden eye within, lest, clouded by the cloud of concealed
sin, it be deprived of the light of Christ.
Going out was easy for no one: each was kept to his own
little cell. Only then was occasion given for the company
to gather, when the accustomed hour of prayer called them all,
and harmony giving praise to God from the heart;
or when, breaking their fast for their weary limbs,
they returned at a fixed time to the common tables,
so that the very sparing time of a modest supper might divide
the end of the finished day, the flesh now tamed,
from the labour that followed in a night spent in vigil.
Only for the sick, the rule being relaxed, was it allowed
to taste unmixed wine, so that the scent of wine poured into cups
might sustain the wasting of an ailing body.
Many had clothing woven of camel's hair,
which would touch their wakeful limbs with light prickings,
shutting out light sleep with pricked flesh,
lest soft fleeces should nourish a slack body
and lascivious clothing flow loose in thin covering,
such as the plenty of their former life had been used to.
For a wise resolve had drawn many there, famous
from ancient blood, to such a life.
So it is the more to be wondered at that, after silken couches and cushions,
this clothing and such severity pleased those who entered.
In the end, wondering at the marks of such ways,
neighbouring peoples and nearby cities sought holy men
from here as their rulers with vying zeal,
so that the teaching of God, flowing from such a spring,
might scatter watering streams into the inmost parts of the thirsty.
But now the time has come to touch at least a small part
of so great a mass of mighty works of power.
And although the disciple's records may adorn the titles of upright virtue
and it is his to set forth beforehand the course of what was done,
yet I shall touch on a very few of [Martin's] own deeds,
showing the greatest praises through brief signs.
There happened to be a tomb nearby, which the vain superstition
of its worshippers, falsely deceived, had often consecrated
as a martyr's, always paying it renowned honour.
Indeed, earlier bishops had even dedicated a venerable altar
[there] before, so that the cult might remain more firmly
founded, strengthened by the added worship of sacred rites.
But after Martin took up the reins laid upon him
and received the holy governance of the people entrusted [to him],
he at once inquires into the name and titles of the martyr
to be venerated, and at what time he had earned
the lineage of so bright a palm, or under what kind of judge.
But when no record appears that could reveal the truth
and all antiquity refuses to know this,
he declines to believe such great things on doubtful words,
nor is the tale of a lying crowd enough for faith.
So he resolves, in matters doubtful and without the weight of a witness,
to seek counsel from the Lord, to whom, ever subject,
times stand present even when the ages have run past.
He hastens to the tomb accompanied by a few, so that, attested
by them, the miracles might win the belief of many.
So when the mass of the adjoining sepulchre was touched,
beside the cold ashes of the dissolved flesh
prayers went back to heaven: the traces of the flesh
are joined to the tomb, but the mind passes even the stars.
Then, having prayed to the Lord with all the strength of faith
that he would reveal to the ignorant the merit and name of the one buried,
suddenly he looks back to his left at a filthy shade,
which with mournful face showed a blackened form
and displayed the most grievous fates of punished criminals,
confused and guilty, with a trembling countenance.
A voice too, given out in the tearful words of one grieving,
uttered frequent sighs in complaints such as these:
'Let the ancient error cease to add punishment
to shades already to be lamented, by giving [me] a title not my own,
lest, for one who has punishment enough from his crime alone,
this burden should grow, doubled by the honour added.
And would that the saints, to whom this homage is rightly
paid, would deign to sprinkle with a slender drop our
flames, the unending burnings of the wretched.
They, rejoicing, enjoy perpetual light;
a dreadful chaos has fenced us in with eternal darkness.
The confusion of night is far from the merits of light.'
This voice reached the ears of many far and wide,
but the form was revealed to Martin alone, whose
lighter mind passed beyond the weights of fragile flesh,
seeing through the bodily mass by the light of the heart.
At once the altar was removed, and all the vain
superstition that had counterfeited sacred rites was driven out.
The mysteries, transferred, migrate to true worship.
What like these achievements will it ever be able to set beside them,
the art infected with magic tricks or steeped in poisons,
weaving lying spells of composed words
and probing stinking entrails with their veins inspected,
so that through the sought-out silences of Tartarean night
a mad demon bellows with a deceitful murmur,
assuming a feigned face under a thin image?
Here surely a simple spirit and the mere piety
of one praying dissolved the bonds of infernal law,
and though the limbs were pressed by the mass of the sepulchre,
yet the confession lived on to the present time.
Nor indeed is this the end of his achievements, nor even for a short
time do the lineages of his powers cease, interrupted.
For grace always clings to the saint as an inseparable companion
and is not confined by any fixed limit of places.
It follows him going forth, remains undivided with him remaining,
and if there is cause for a journey, it gladly accompanies him going.
For while he was hastily passing through the trackless parts of a wide countryside,
where wild Gaul lies spread out in broad plains,
while a pagan crowd was following a wretched corpse
and the linen cloths, set trembling, were moved by a light wind,
with his gaze stretched far over the open plains
he thinks the funeral procession is the worship of an unspeakable
demon, and the rites of wretched sacred things carried
on the necks of revellers, bowed beneath idol figures.
At once he raises the holy and venerable sign,
and with the cross set against them blocks those hurrying on,
and halts their unsteady steps by the weight of the standard.
Then indeed the wretches, held by a torpor laid upon them,
could be seen, their limbs stiffened, their sinews bound,
very many efforts frustrated, their members entangled,
their steps slowed, their pace fixed motionless,
the crowds hemmed in, enclosed by a commanded boundary,
and the barriers of a wall not to be crossed, stretched before them,
setting an immense enclosure against them on all sides,
until little by little, with a nearer view, it became plain
that it was an honour paid to funeral rites. Then again by the same
standard and by the sign itself freedom was restored.
Thus by the command of the cross and the power of faith together
he had the right to bind the wanderers and to loose the bound.
Gathering up these things touched on in haste, because the abundance
of his powers urges [me] to touch with brief signs what must be praised,
lest a most worthless page should delay minds hastening
toward such great miracles with long-winded words,
I am caught up again by the weight of greater matters.
Once, its roof cast down, he had levelled a sacrilegious temple
to the ground, crushing the idols with the broken beams
and pressing down the images under the whole ruin.
A pine near this place, spreading wide, opened its green
branches, and its aged arms far and wide
had woven a green forest on its leafy crown,
and with its lattice of leaves the dense grove of a single tree
kept off all heat: a perennial shade
covered a constant mildness in a counterfeit spring.
This pine too he sets about joining to the ruins of the temple,
desiring to roll into a like grave
whatever drew the hearts of the wretched into error.
Then indeed the senseless madness of the inflamed crowd
strives to come quickly to the aid of the beloved wood
and with every effort to prevent the pious wish.
Reason avails nothing to the mad, holy words nothing to profane
minds, no voice to the deaf, no light to the blind.
It is cried out that things cannot bring salvation to a man
which cannot avail themselves; that the lords of wood cannot be
helped by wood: these things serve the nod of him
who would serve [God], being subject [only] to what is subject [to him], the same man
picking from the woods what is to be burned, leaving what is to be revered.
Against this they cry out, wanting things far different,
their hearts deeply steeped in idol poison:
'Stop forcing the unwilling with long-winded words.
If you prove by deeds what you would persuade, this condition
will rightly please, and bring belief: we ourselves will at once
set about quickly cutting down our pine.
You, if you offer true proofs of faith, as it falls
receive it, and gladly run to meet the collapse you desire,
trusting the Lord that nothing grievous [will befall you].' So harsh
a condition is accepted, and the most just man did not refuse the unjust mouth,
trusting in the power of God, who has the ready ability
even to forbid with a word a collapse already at hand.
Without delay bonds are tied tight about his limbs,
and, to be crushed, he is now placed on that side
where the trunk hung leaning with its whole stem,
and now, its branches bending with swaying weight,
it threatened what lay below with the mass of a certain fall.
Rivalling joys press on with all their wishes.
They press on with ceaseless blows and frequent double axes.
Hope close at hand supplies spirit and strength to the weary.
Vengeance shuts out feeling, anger drives off pain.
The monks grow pale, half dead, and greater is the danger
to faith, too greatly confounded by such terror,
until, overcome little by little by its wounds, [the pine] gave a crash
as it leaned, and, driven with its whole leap toward the saint,
the hastening wishes outran the swift frenzy,
his limbs now almost shattered by the whirl so near.
He, faith forbidding fear, dread driven out,
awaiting the near collapse with a steadfast heart,
lest unbelief, seeing the pine turned too soon,
should put the work down to chance and deny the merit,
thinking it a mere occurrence: but now, with the danger closer,
raises his right hand, armed with the protection of the sign,
and sets the cross against it. By this at once all its force
is broken, and, swiftly called back in a rapid turn,
the pine is borne in a swift whirl to the opposite side
upon the authors of the crime. Those exulting close by
trembled and feared the collapse turned upon themselves:
those who believed they had carefully chosen a safe place
for so great a spectacle, scarcely recovering their wits,
see their seats pierced through by shattered branches.
A shout is raised to heaven, and the regions echo,
astonished, and voices are returned from the whole gathering:
the monks bear witness to joy, the vanquished to miracles.
The tongue sounds Christ; Christ together, with kindly mouth,
the ignorant and the knowing sing: this party acknowledges
the favour, that one seeks faith. So suddenly a harmonious
will among the discordant, Christ uniting them,
both earned the gift of faith and persuaded them to believe.
For certainly there was no one at all in that throng
who did not carry off the gifts of the hoped-for salvation,
added to the Lord's flocks by the protection of the sign,
and the places that, covered with foul shrines, had stunk,
Mother Church soon covered over with true temples.
Thus you conquer, Martin, thus you overwhelm your enemies,
thus your heavy sentence tramples the oppressed: those
who were harsh a merciful victory made brothers.
So the outcome sharpens his mind, and a happy victory
constantly nourishes his zeal for conquering the rebellious.
For scarcely were the idols smoking, the flames sunk down,
and fine ashes flying from the nearby fire,
when the burning of a similar temple is renewed once more
by his most just right hand, exulting in frequent flames.
But while the whirlwind sows blazing heat far and wide,
and fiercely seethes in frequent waves
the madness of the flames, belching a rushing cloud,
increasing its gathered fury with the nearby destruction,
it makes with its whole column for a house not far removed,
licking the nearby roofs with deadly flames.
When the saint, alarmed, saw the danger pressing
and that the fires, now mingled with the scorched beams,
had surrounded the house, wrapped in a whirlpool of flames,
hastening, he climbs the roof with a swift leap,
where the densest ball of fire presses on the house with its excess,
and offers his limbs, set against them, to the oncoming flames.
Then indeed the fires, bent back by a contrary blast,
return into the wind, and although the storm presses,
the greater force of the command drives and compels
the raging wind at once to yield to the turned-back fires.
Thus nature, overpowered, obeys the merits of the one commanding.
Flames are not driven by gusts, but gusts by flames,
and the fire, following commands, so dealt with both,
seizing what was decreed to it, leaving what was defended.
Thus, the temple having been vanquished by a just burning,
they go to demolish another, which Leprosus,
once a wealthy village, used to worship with perverse mind.
But after the frenzied madness of the thronging crowd
had driven back the attempted work, and the whirlwind of violent uproar
had set all its fury against the undertaking,
he goes back to the pathless seclusion of lonely places,
and there presses on more forcefully with holy prayers,
his intent of praying carrying on through three days
and joining to them as many hours of nights kept in vigil.
Moreover, covered in a garment woven of bristles,
he pricked his wasted limbs with constant sharpness,
so that the too-rough clothing wore away his thin skin
and the skin, at their touch, dreaded the projecting spikes;
he struck the stony ground with bones harder than it,
prolonged the slow days into late fasts,
drenched his whole face with a river of tears,
so that the ever-constant mercy of Christ the Lord,
greatly pitying the toil of his innocent servant,
might give fulfilment to his prayer and accomplish what he had attempted,
wholly removing the endeavours of the opposing side.
Meanwhile he sees standing nearby armed
men in angelic brightness, and recognition does not
dawn slowly: their familiar look gives ready confidence,
and moreover he is told in words the reason for their coming:
that he should not tremble, nor fear force, nor dread weapons,
recognising by such signs a favour present to him;
whatever crowd might rise up in opposing uproar,
the help of God was enough, who could at once
vanquish all the bands by the power of his word;
that they at once brought help and carried back commands.
So his spirit, keener, its strength fully recovered,
believing these arms of the two sufficient for the war,
he regains strength for the work begun, and into the midst of the bands
burst the constancy restored to his trembling heart.
The temples are laid low, overturned in utter ruin;
the fallen images receive the whole mass,
and the shattered idols sink beneath the thrown-down roofs.
Mingled dust enveloped everything alike together,
beams, altars, statues, mortar, stones, metal.
Nor indeed does anyone, come forward from so great a throng,
make ready to go against him. He remains undaunted,
seeing the hearts of the trembling men vanquished.
The people wait motionless. The breasts of those threatening
grew stiff, and their insides were stunned, their vitals thunderstruck.
Their limbs bring forth no movement, their words no uproar:
the wretches' limbs went rigid, the voice stuck in their throats,
the hands of those attempting fell, and the shouting of those gaping.
As the sea, which the whirlwind of a violent storm,
bearing down on the waves, has stirred, torn up from the lowest depth,
dashes all the rocks with foaming spray
and with hoarse roar rises over the banks set against it,
while the broken masses beat the hollow shores
and the nearby shallows mingle all the deep:
soon, when the gusts have fallen silent, their motion laid aside,
an immense plain of calm waters is spread out,
the smooth marble surface settles as the wind is laid,
and the changed face of the unmoving element lies still,
inviting light boats onto the levelled flood:
not otherwise did the madness of the furious crowd fall silent,
and it laid its storm to rest and let go its blasts,
and, submissive, cried out only this, in true words:
that Martin's Lord was to be worshipped by the whole world together,
that they knew him alone as God. For if deaf
idols could ever confer salvation on one who asks,
they would have brought it to themselves; nor does anyone give a gift
that he lacks: rather, he who asks the needy is the poorer.
Thus, the brightness of the true light received deep within,
this crowd too, devoted to the holy camp, swelled its ranks.
His heart continually invigorated by such triumphs,
he longs for battles again: increased faith removes fear,
hope of merit gives him spirit, dread of danger gives way.
For soon a like cause stirred a like uproar,
when a rustic folk, exceedingly mad, hurried to rescue
a temple that was to be overthrown, and increased its usual
stubbornness with the immense weight of headlong fury.
Indeed, madness had so overwhelmed all their sense
that a certain man ran up threatening with drawn sword,
daring to brandish the sacrilegious steel to wound.
And when the saint, joyfully throwing back his covering,
offered his bared neck, that man, not drawing back at all,
rises in fury to the sword raised high.
He lifted his mad right hand higher into the air,
raising his whole body with a swift effort,
pressing on with hurried steps in headlong striving,
so that the blow, coming from higher, might fall more violently:
when suddenly his insides went rigid, his sinews bound fast,
and the movement stuck, spent in the thin air,
and the outstretched right hand held up the steel in vain,
and the whole blow perished in his numbed limbs,
and the hand stayed fixed, its effort mocked.
Then his limbs, collapsing backwards with their whole weight,
fell headlong to the ground in a precipitous fall,
and the bones resounded, crushed beneath the battered limbs,
and lay face down on the mound of stony earth.
Then at last groans were wrung out and tears forced,
and, threats laid aside, the most pitiable entreaty
of the suppliant turned and came back to seek a healing pardon.
Why, I ask, did you call back your greedy hand from blood?
Why do you spare one for whom no one pleads? What holds back your blow,
if your anger remains? You surely do not wish to forgive:
why do you hold back the steel? See, the innocent neck lies open,
bared for your wounds: why do you delay your wishes,
you who have the mind of one striking? Why, with the crime intact,
is vengeance put off? Even if your right hand is idle, you are doing
what you desire to have done. If the will is not changed,
the guilt remains: the verdict of the heart is enough for desert.
Nor indeed was it from this alone that the trembling breasts
of the astonished people saw the gifts of preserved safety.
For soon, when a like madness was bringing a like death
with drawn weapon, suddenly struck away,
the steel's blade deserts the striker with an empty blow,
and the frantic right hand searched for the weapon wrenched from it,
and the deceived eyes saw all the wishes of gathered fury
vanish with the loss of the steel.
Yet at times he was accustomed to persuade with healing
address, and to change fierce minds with words,
and to soften hardened hearts with holy speech,
lighting up the ancient night with the light of teaching.
Besides, it was easy for him to restore health
to the sick, walking to the lame, and sight to the blind.
For certainly the violence of no illness, however great, had so
overwhelmed anyone that he did not carry away the comforts
of longed-for health, rejoicing to grow strong again once he had seen the saint.
This can be made clear even by the present deed.
Once, within the walls of Trier, an unmarried maiden
had wasted away, consumed by a grievous illness, paralysed,
and her numbed limbs lacked all movement,
deprived of their functions. Already, the flesh forsaken,
a thin breath was breathing in her cold breast.
Her frightened kin grew pale at death so near
and watered her withered limbs with a fountain of tears,
and the sad honour to be paid at the funeral
had gathered the mournful band of attendants: when, into the murmurs of the weepers,
a messenger bursts in excitedly, his mouth opened wide,
reporting that Martin had come, who had the ready power
to grant the wished-for cure by holy prayers.
As soon as this word came to the sorrowing ears of the father,
he flies there half-dead and throws himself at [Martin's] knees, begging
for help, and sprinkles his feet with abundant weeping,
and sighs break his sobbing words,
and his tears speak more of his prayers than his words do.
But the saint, strong in modest piety, on the other hand,
shares his feeling but denies his own merit. He refuses to admit he has
the power to give aid, but in his heart he shares
the grief. He shuns display, but weeps over the misfortune,
and proves his merit by avoiding it. Thus he stands out higher
through a humble heart. He adds to praise what he takes from honour.
Seeing this, the father presses all the more vehemently,
until, moved by constant and just asking,
the holy entreaty of the priests, joined to the father's prayers,
compelled the reluctant man by a gentle right
to visit the sorrowful inner rooms of the grieving parent.
The people stand before the doors: the hanging breasts
of the astonished folk await the miracles of Christ.
When he, full of pity, saw the wasted limbs of the half-dead girl
and her eyes languishing from the ills that had consumed her,
the skin clinging to the bones of the dried-up body
and the colour of the skin spoiled by bile poured into it,
and, the murmur of the tightly bound tongue wholly withdrawn,
that she breathed a scanty breath from an icy breast,
and that the threads of the veins, dying with broken pulse,
their rhythm cut off, were forsaking the searching hand:
at once, prone with his whole body, to the ground
he throws himself, asking from the Lord the medicine of the word,
for whom to have commanded is enough, and to overcome [medical] art with a nod.
He felt that God was present. He asks for oil to be brought out.
On the liquid offered a holy blessing is laid.
Then, rejoicing in the ointment of the changed fluid,
he touches each limb with the healing chrism.
The holy right hand, applied, drives out the old pain,
and the happy gifts of health obtained,
poured in, gradually return at the physician's touch.
So, the illnesses having been driven from every part of the limbs,
strength is restored and takes their place in the invigorated body.
Soon the girl rises up strong, while the people marvel,
and, setting her steps firmly by the divine gift,
gives praise to Christ the Lord at the holy altars.
After this work of power had filled the walls, crowded
with throngs, all ran up eagerly,
whose minds a demon or whose bodies a disease
had overwhelmed, begging a cure for heart and limbs.
Some went away firm in their step, others sound in their mind.
Yet chiefly among all the miracles which the grace of Christ
deigned to work through its servant,
the immediate healing of one slave stood out,
whom a demon held captive with full right.
Indeed, when the saint, moved by the great entreaty of those asking,
ordered the wretch to be brought to the holy
threshold, no one could bind the raging man.
So, raving with frenzied mouth, he drove them all away,
gnashing his teeth: blood had covered his torn body
all over, and wounds bristled on his naked limbs.
Then his master, exalted by very great distinction,
adorned with the fasces of a proconsul, forgetful of this
dignity, comes and throws himself at the kindly knees,
and, prone at his feet, wraps his coaxing arms around them,
begging that, since neither force nor chains could avail
to bring the servant raving with maddened heart,
he himself would come to the house in which for a long time now
a constant guard had kept the slave shut up.
But the saint refused to tread the threshold of a profane man,
nor would the righteous one go in under idolatrous beams,
setting the stench of a temple apart from the chrism of Christ.
But he, clinging violently to the saint's holy knees,
promises that, once his servant was healed, he would be willing to believe
whatever the teaching of so great a master should hand down.
Then at last, moved by so just a plea from the one asking,
he carried his longed-for steps to the threshold that was to be saved,
and the same medicine brought help to the master, who prayed so justly,
as to the servant. Both give thanks:
the one rejoicing at faith received, the other at his mind restored.
And straightway after these miracles a new deed
roused the astonished people to such great proclamations.
For by chance, entering the threshold of a neighbouring house,
he cries out that he sees in the very doorway the foul
shade of a raging demon, horrible even to see.
Without delay, at once the enemy, now betrayed,
began to rage, having seized a cook, and to throw into tumult
the inner chambers of the house, to gnash with his jaws,
and to bare the menacing teeth of the captive mouth,
exercising his inborn wrath with another's bites,
while the demon's madness, mingled in, shakes the possessed body,
so that the frenzy of the demon rages with a human mouth,
armed for its own furies with another's tooth.
They scatter in fear, and no one dares
to stand against him, and examples sharpen their utmost fears.
But the saint, trusting in the Lord, laughs at the straggling
crowds and with a swift advance offers himself in [the demon's] path.
Indeed, while the madness was shaking the trembling jaws,
clashing the wretched teeth with a deathly growl
and renewing repeated bites with a nodding head,
he resolutely thrust his fingers into the gaping throat,
halting the most savage powers of the hostile robber.
The greedy jaws stuck fast, the wound held off,
the shameless fury of the wide-open mouth froze, suspended,
the tongue beneath rejoiced at the healing touch,
and soft kisses pressed the right hand inserted there.
Then, because, with the mouth blocked, no escape lay open,
[the demon], expelled by a flux of the bowels, left the innards
emptied, and drew only stench out of the body.
Meanwhile, suddenly, the whole city is thrown into
tumult. A wicked rumour brings [word of] barbarian movements,
scattering countless fears through credulous hearts.
Yet there was no messenger of this rumour,
so that the report could be shown credible by a clear source.
So when he saw that such flames were being stirred by such doubtful matters
and that the peoples were held by an uncertain terror,
he commands the demon shut up in the captive body
to disclose from where the tale had scattered this new rumour.
At once, driven by the word as by a torturer, he cries out
that he confesses himself the cause, the crime and the head of the evils:
that he, with his fellow spirits, had sown these lies
to oppress the fearful people with dread.
So this true confession of a lying robber,
with the demon tormented, freed the sorrowing minds.
But now, to recount the deeds of such great goodness,
neither will my barren mind suffice nor my worthless page.
O truly neighbouring goods, ready compassion
and a humble mind! He who loves all spurns no one.
For wicked leprosy had covered a certain man with a horrible disease,
staining all his flesh with a covering of blotches
and scattering thick spots over the corrupted body.
Since the frequent disgust of the healthy marked him out,
and the most unjust mind, unaware of its own possible fate,
despised the grievous diseases in another's body,
the saint, entering the gate with a crowd going before him,
such as had gathered to do homage to so great a patron
and was thronging the threshold of the walls in dense crowds,
gives kisses to the wretched man, joined to him in face and mouth,
and, not fearing that his face would be defiled by such a touch,
pressed the seals of peace upon the joined lips.
The others' minds were stunned. But he, rejoicing,
felt in the touch the gifts of divine bounty,
and swift health returning quickly through his limbs,
and a quick radiance spreading through his renewed flesh.
O truly precious is the favour of your peace,
and the medicine that always flows from your holy mouth!
Whether you touch limbs with your lips or hearts with your speech,
your kisses will heal the sick, and your words those to be taught.
And would that a like mercy might touch our diseases,
and that Martin, praying, might be willing with so holy a mouth
to drive off the blotches of a wretched heart.
Then, I believe, I would be called back to the joys of true peace,
lifting my healed face to the holy mysteries,
and, after squandering the wealth that my portion had given,
my hope would hang upon the mouth of a merciful Lord,
and, leaving the food of swine or the joys of the flesh,
I would receive the sure seals of true faith.
Indeed, even a mere touch, or the fringe of his garment,
and threads snatched in rivalry from the torn wool
brought swift cures in all cases.
For, to pass over the deeds which, done no less plainly
for humble men, have lain hidden, will, I ask, he lie hidden,
Arborius, who held the world's highest honour,
who, illustrious at the summit of the lofty prefecture,
ruled the Roman government with the reins entrusted to him,
and was no less outstanding in the uprightness of his pious character?
His only daughter, now wasting, her limbs thoroughly consumed,
had thrown her feeble frame upon her bed;
a fever, returning with an unbroken law of recurrence
on the fourth day, had so stripped her of the cloak of flesh,
always repeating its frequent onslaughts,
that her afflicted body could feel no relief
even in the days between, with the fever close at hand,
since the past bout claims one day for itself,
and the other suffers in dread the onslaught to come.
So while her father, with sorrowful love, cherished such a girl,
and while the frequent panting of the father's mouth
ran over her icy limbs with warm breath,
a letter was delivered and reached his trembling right hand,
which the holy bishop was sending to his grieving friend.
When he, rejoicing at the gift of the page he had read through,
pressed kisses joyfully upon the absent right hand,
he closed the venerable roll with a quick movement
and, hurrying, quickly laid it on [her] panting breast.
O truly precious faith! The fever is driven off
and put to flight, and the flame of fiery heat is removed.
The present blessing penetrates the parched veins
and waters the exhausted marrow with the dew of the words,
restoring swift health by the Lord's goodness:
to whose praise we shall rightly, rejoicing, refer
what we now marvel that faithful servants have been able [to do].
Nor did this medicine grant healing to the limbs alone,
but faith, increased, added true health to the heart.
For at once the virgin, vowed to God, is offered through him
to the Lord, through whom, rescued from disease, she has strength.
Thus the grace of this gift was granted to three at once:
the bishop consecrates, the father offers, the virgin is consecrated.
Indeed, a like medicine restored health to Paulinus also,
whom the glory of his remarkable faith has raised
far and wide. His sight was then hidden by a cloud drawn over it,
and a darkness stretched out, with shadows poured in,
shut out all light with a covering of blotches.
This a sponge, light and held with a delicate touch,
put to flight, by the nearby gift of the blessed right hand,
barely brought to the eye. His sight, now restored, learned
to bear the light, and in wonder received new light.
And would that the medicine of the holy patron would deign
to touch the darkness of our heart with such light,
so that it might again reproduce the mysteries of the ancient deed:
the same name, and the same physician, an equal cause for healing.
We marvel indeed, seeing so many great
remedies of the pious chief physician. Let us marvel too at that
healing which the physician earned, with Christ as physician,
through whom, being generous and at the same time grateful for the gift,
the good man rejoices in gifts both spent and kept.
For, striving to climb up to the high part
where the building hung, supported on tall columns,
while he set slipping steps on the ladder, headlong
he fell, and, renewing his fall again and again on the rungs,
collapsed and struck the ground with his body bruised.
But see, while his broken limbs, exhausted, groan
in fierce pain, bringing sudden comfort to the afflicted man,
an angel stands by, venerable with holy face,
hastening to wash the wounds with poured water,
gradually touching [them] with the ointment of an unknown juice,
spreading the thin liquid with a gentle touch.
From this the moistened limbs quickly felt swift healing,
the body softened at once, its veins moistened,
and immediately the limbs grew firm and strong; the pains, put to flight
on every side, gave way at the Lord's command.
Swift steps, a lively mind, joy of heart and of mouth,
a face in harmony with a grateful breast.
While he praises the Lord, he claims nothing for himself from it,
and revealed his merit, because he denied that he had merited [it].
BOOK THREE.
Where are you calling me again, barren reed, and voice that sends
whistling from broken straws? This glory surely
deserves to swell the voices of greater trumpets,
nor could so great a sound burst from small stalks
as would be able to fill even lofty clarions.
But if so narrow a pipe were helped by even a slender breath,
one sent by the blessing of the holy mouth,
if it cannot speak great things, it will at least speak sweet ones.
So the first part of the book will be held by ambition
defeated. This door will unlock the remaining praises,
by which, after degenerate fears through many ages,
lost liberty shone forth in a corrupted world.
Once Maximus, elated by wars waged successfully,
and proud now from the death of one lord
and the exile of another, had increased by success the crime
clinging wickedly to his character, and prosperity, more
unhappy for a proud heart, had often reopened the wounds of a depraved
nature, prosperity that was to fall more heavily amid good fortune.
So to this king, from different regions, came in numbers
the shepherds of God, whose perpetual care [was]
either to keep or to feed the Lord's pious people,
striving to release the accused, to free those in chains,
to give rest to the weary, comfort to the sorrowful,
to ask a homeland for exiles and to plead for pardon,
to obtain for the wretched proscribed their property and their life.
And while they strove to hasten these things with kindly zeal,
little by little the holy dignity of the fathers, submitting with fearful assent
to the swollen [king], began to grow far too cheap,
given over to flatteries, not such as the ancient dignity of priests
had been accustomed to pay, but the foul ambition
of clients, debased at the nod of a swollen patron.
Among them Martin alone, with steadfast heart and mouth,
stained his pious inmost self with no false colour,
nor did fearful cowardice weigh down with an ugly blemish
a mind humble toward Christ, lofty toward the heights of the world.
Indeed, steadfastly exerting himself in those very petitions,
if there was then any cause to entreat the swollen king,
he obtained the wish of one requesting as if by the right of one commanding.
Often, too, with frequent pleading, ambition set out to move
the holy man, so that he would at least come late,
after being asked so many times, to the king's spurned banquets.
For he, scorning arrogance and turning over [the king's] deeds,
refused altogether to join himself to the table of one
to whose crimes he thought it sinful to bind his holy mind
even by the faintest assent,
charging him with the slaughter of his lords, with an empire
won by blood, the death of a king and the reign of a tyrant.
But when, wearying that pious heart with continual pleas,
he washed away his guilt, and, clearing himself of the charges and crimes,
said that the government of the empire had been laid on him
by the terror of those who ordered it, and that it was wrong for a power
wrested by sword and arms to be weighed down by the burden of ill will,
[a power] free of ambition; and that indeed no small signs of his favour
had the Lord sent in so great a triumph,
and that no man of faith, however lukewarm and small,
was unaware that the turns of waging war
hang on the nod of God; and that it is all the more manifest,
if the one inferior in strength and men conquers the one who trusted more in numbers,
that he has conquered with Christ as judge;
and that indeed he had done nothing bloody, even after the wars,
with a harsh spirit, and that the fury of the sword
had had no force after the battle line; that after arms and trumpets
the guiltless swords had ceased from the crime of slaughter,
and the peace was spattered with no blood at all.
Repeating such things often and praying more urgently with entreaties,
he softened the holy man's rigour with frequent argument,
so that, pardoning the fault and overcome by his zeal, he went
to the dishes of the royal table he had disdained before.
Hope, now nearer, exults over so great a favour.
The festal day rejoices to shine with a joyful gathering.
Chosen nobles are added, whom the splendour of an honour
close to the royal summit binds to it,
distinguished by their robes of state, holding authority over laws
and arms, either the rights of the courts or the trumpets of war.
In the middle among these, where the sigma-couch bends in its curve,
the priest reclined. On the right and left the rank of powerful
commanders, their limbs placed on golden couch-frames,
pressed the purple of precious fleece spread beneath.
At the king's right hand, venerable with holy countenance,
sat the elder, like Moses when, bringing back the holy laws,
he came down from the sacred summit of the mountain,
flashing with the exceeding brightness of his changed face,
when the splendour of his face displayed the face of his heart
and veils could not hold back the new light.
The rejoicing crowd of attendants marvel in silence,
and the devoted court vies in modest services
to serve so holy a man. All have one care,
the longed-for service; the reverence for the king is less.
Even the king himself, though present, prefers that Martin excel.
Royal dishes crowd the tables set below,
rich purple gleams on the lofty couch-frames,
soft silks stir with crimson dye,
and there glows, from skeins skilfully drawn without wool,
metal softened into threads and mingled with the purple.
Hangings stretched across the proud doorways tremble,
and in the entrances the moving barrier of curtains sways.
All things shine with varied adornment above and below:
