the heights with paint, the floors with marble, the ceilings with metal.
Capacious crystal vessels hold glassy waters,
and since the vessel itself seems both the form of a shell and of the wave,
you would not think its walls could hold the liquid taken in.
Cups are poured from jewels and drunk from jewels,
a mass of electrum sets off the tawny gold.
Art was in the value; the value is more valuable than the art.
These little vessels shine with gems, these stand out with figures;
some are rough to the sight, but smooth to the touch;
and on gleaming platters and broad dishes there are present
the fruits of air and forest, of land and sea.
After hunger was taken away by the feast, then the only wish
was to relieve parched thirst. The attendants snatched up
ice enclosed in gold and snowy waters;
others offered dewy bowls. The care and vigour of the servants
anticipates the wish of those who ask.
Then the king orders the hesitant attendant to offer [the cup] to Martin,
yielding the service, at the same time, with the order reversed,
ardently desiring to follow so holy a hand,
so that the bowl, made more precious by the touch of such lips,
might steep the liquid poured into it with heavenly dew.
But the faintest drop of wine that sprinkled [the cup]
failed upon the lips, barely moistened by the touch.
When the king tried to take the cup with outstretched hand,
he handed it to his own priest, weighing the honour due to faith.
The merit of the heart, not the purple of the king,
prevailed. The diadem yielded to faith preferred above it.
The hearts of the men who watched were stunned, fixed
in astonished minds; and even to the spurned king his constancy
was more pleasing than it was astonishing, nor did the rancour of envy
burn him as he weighed the weight of so great a deed.
What priest, however great, even under a lesser judge,
would dare so much for holy right?
Terror did not overcome the firm, nor favour the just,
nor the eagerness of the host, nor the anger of the powerful.
O virtue neighbour to God: so, with heart withdrawn,
may you be as if far off yourself. To conquer the present world.
Nor did he fear to declare steadfastly to the king himself whatever the kindly
Spirit had revealed to him, filling his pious inmost being with an infused gift,
things not to be doubted:
the varied outcomes of the war, battles at first
fortunate, soon a grim defeat in another contest.
And as his fiery mind saw all these with pure perception,
so a swift outcome proved his words, as if they had been seen.
For in the first contest [the king] overwhelmed and routed his opponent,
soon he bowed his captive neck to the general on his return.
Nor is it wonderful that a keen mind saw so much,
leaving all cares behind with lofty heart
and flying with heavenly perception far above the stars.
For often the faithful monks standing before the doors
were amazed as he mingled words with angelic speech.
Thus his body and limbs felt nothing corporeal or perishable,
and to a mind already enjoying freedom
the weight of the subdued flesh did no harm at all.
The demon himself, too, with whatever face he tried to deceive,
lay open and plain in his futile effort,
and was not permitted to play with changed shapes.
In the end, when no escape at all lay open to him in his alarm,
he would breathe out his savage poison through raging words,
desiring to inflame with words the man unharmed by his snares,
to tear with the venom of his tongue one who had slipped from his teeth,
pouring out futile rage with his efforts already broken.
Indeed, shaking his right hand dripping with pitiable blood
and displaying the crime of slaughter on his bloody horn,
glad at the evil and laughing at grim things,
he burst into the holy cell with a deadly muttering,
pouring out a hellish voice through insolent words:
'See,' he said, 'at last the proofs of my fury fulfilled.
Chance gave these arms; violently I drove this weapon home,
conquering through the service of a beast, but by my crime.
So that the fruit of the crime may be greater, that man of yours and of your
flock has fallen to console our anger,
renewing my exhausted strength with longed-for blood.'
At once he orders all the elders summoned quickly
to visit the monks' cells with swift concern,
in case the lying words of the deceitful brigand
had for once told the truth about his own crime,
such as the voice of wretched criminals is wont to be
when, under the cruel torturer, they confess deeds deserving punishment.
Then they report that none at all of the brothers
was marked by that charge; that they had at once counted before them
the whole flock of the saints, who, shut in the fold,
scorned the rage of the wolves gnashing at the barriers,
the flock which watchful Martin was nourishing for the eternal King;
but that one man had set out after receiving a fee
to keep off the cold with wood brought in by cart.
Martin orders that he be met with speed, believing
that he, made then a companion to the monks even through trade,
had lain open to the snares of the brigand who had confessed.
Without delay the conjecture is proved at once.
Going out, they see, not far from the threshold, the wretched man half-dead,
breathing out the last breaths of life.
Yet he, opening his eyes faint with death,
barely, with the broken murmur of a sobbing tongue,
drew a faint voice from his icy breast,
explaining the cause of the wound. For by chance a bullock,
while its loosened bonds were being tightened with straps,
too free with its roaming neck and rebellious against its master,
had pierced his soft groin with its hellish horn.
After he had told this and fallen silent with closed lips,
then he laid down his head, wearied by death, and a saffron pallor
spread over his face and limbs in his icy body.
By this end he perished. Yet for us this end too
showed the merit of Martin, who was permitted to know the future
so well that the veils of the flesh did nothing at all
to slow his swift mind with earthly weight.
In vain the exceedingly lying and cunning enemy
would try either to hide his frauds in snares or to deceive with shapes,
wasting these efforts so many times to no purpose,
daring to imitate the forms of feigned gods,
and to feign the likeness of those whose honour he feigned,
now portraying the incestuous face of Jupiter and the fury of Mars,
Mercury with his feet bound with false wings,
Vulcan with his tongs, or Phoebus with the plectrum of his strings,
mad Minerva with shield and crests,
wanton Venus, Diana shaking the thickets,
the sister incestuous by the unlawful law of the marriage bed,
losing even the name of sister through her brother's crime.
Displaying in such forms the deeds worthy of his own [gods]
and betraying his own crimes with a false face,
he could in no way slip away, but, his fraud uncovered,
the mocked demon lost his cunning efforts,
breathing out his last poison through insolent words
and provoking with vices or voice the man unharmed.
Patience, bearing all these things with unmoved face,
scorning flatteries, laughing at abuse and insults,
and recognising the enemy as deceitful in either fiction,
could neither be wounded by reproach nor moved by praise,
setting the signs of salvation against the darts of words
and breaking the brigand's weapons by the interposed cross.
He, often attacking the pious heart with harsh complaints,
the impious one dared, alas, to reproach the pious man
with love of mercy, resounding thus in his voice openly,
so that his deadly words were plain to many witnesses.
'Why,' he said, 'if you condemn crimes, do you receive those hateful to the Lord,
and, blaming vice, seek the company
of sinners? Perhaps the deeds of your people are hidden from you,
done then at my urging, very many of which I prompted
and in which I had a great part. Who, I ask, will approve
a man hostile to deeds yet fair to those who do them?'
He said: 'Serpent swollen with ancient venom,
this is not the judgment of Christ the Lord concerning the wretched,
who, if he sees guilt ended, casts away anger,
setting no times for punishment except the time of the offence,
warning that sins should not remain, remitting them when ended,
gentle to things past, if there is present amendment,
calling back the straying, granting pardon of crimes to those called back,
patient with the perverse, merciful and gentle to those who return:
life of men, death of sins, compassionate to both,
he bids the destruction of wickedness be the cause of salvation.
Nor would I despair, trusting in [his] proven goodness,
that, although your crimes surpass all offences,
you without whom no one does anything wicked, and who to all
[...] mixed in sins, deservedly [...] to mix in punishments.
if you would grieve for your misdeeds, at least, even late,
mercy would snatch you from the midst of the flames.'
O blessed piety, that anyone should trust so much
in the goodness of the Lord God as kindly to promise
even things which he admits have not been promised,
while he tries to call back from his accustomed crime
the very author of crime, removing sin from its tinder
and cutting back the hateful stock from its first root.
But since, striving to sing frequent triumphs,
our murmurings have touched the tyrant of Tartarus,
and amid the titles of praise, wishing to unfold
the series of wars, we have sounded the enemy's name,
this too we shall tell in such speech as Christ has given,
a thing done at that time which we greatly marvel at.
Once, joined to the companions of the saint and the ministers of Christ,
a young man, Clarus [bright] in deed and in name,
had set his cell not far from the holy teacher,
taking many brothers into a righteous fellowship,
so that a harmonious symphony might sing psalms in holy hymns
and concordant glory resound from joined tongues.
A certain crafty young man, bearing pretences
and fictions of contrived deceits, and feigning the whole
appearance of an innocent, deceiving under the name of monk,
sought him out, in sheep's clothing but with the mind of wolves,
breathing the ancient venom from his corrupted breast.
And at first, mingled with the saints in body alone,
the pretender acted out a show of the common life.
Afterwards, accustomed to boast of angelic conversations,
he had raised his lying mind to vain heights,
to fall the farther from the summit of a proud heart.
Indeed, persuading by prodigies, he compelled unwary
hearts, as though his merits were already proven by evidence,
to believe his swollen words the more on account of slight signs.
At times he used to boast of the Lord's own
address to him, as though a frequent messenger
constantly brought [word] back to him from the heavenly seat,
displaying great favour by familiar speech.
Nor did he fear to compare himself with the holy prophets,
breathing the lying words of a deceitful brigand.
And now indeed many to believe his fabricated words
he had driven. Alone, with steadfast heart, Clarus
repelled the lying murmurs from his holy mind,
and though the madman feigned the anger of the Lord,
he could neither frighten the grave man nor deceive the cautious one,
though he promised that his power would be proven by many signs.
For so that miracles might capture deceived minds,
he chose to confound the astonished with such words:
'This night, I say, God, so that the grace
he has willed to decree for our merits may not be thought vain,
will grant me to be clad in the fleece of a snow-white garment.
When these gifts lie plainly open to your eyes,
at least, if you hesitate to believe words, believe
what you see, and readily praise the favour you behold.'
Then indeed [there was] wakeful expectation of so great a portent,
of where the course of the foretold novelty would lead.
And lo, now at about the time of midnight,
when, dividing them, it looks not far off toward each day,
nearest to the coming one and not far removed from the one left behind,
the earth shook and trembled, a vast crash on every side
thundered horribly, and in the darkness a fouler fire
flashed with a terrible torch and a counterfeit light.
Trembling hearts are terrified by the sudden sight.
At once then, eager and keener from the very success
by which the course of the foretold fraud had thus advanced,
he gave the fleece to someone to touch and to see.
He quickly summoned the rest, lest it deceive only one,
the new form of contrived trickery. Those called were amazed,
close at hand, at the garment, remarkable for whiteness and purple,
and at the weave yielding softly to their anxious hands,
as they ran over the soft threads of the fine web.
Yet it could not be recognised from what fleece
the garment was drawn, though it gleamed when brought close,
but the garment, seen by the eye or believed by touch,
kept, lying in both, the form it had assumed.
Then Clarus urged them all with wholesome exhortation
that, with things so confounded by enormous portents,
they should return to the Lord with prayers, since he alone
could betray the hidden deceits and bring the brigand's fraud
out of its darkness. Swiftly the whole wakeful
throng flies to the accustomed psalms, sweet melodies,
and seeks comfort in holy hymns,
so as to drive off sluggish sleep with invigorated body
and overcome the silence of night with sacred songs.
Tears follow psalms, sighs follow the voice:
the heart cries out if the tongue is silent; all
the time is joined in praise of the Lord, by turns of mind and mouth.
Meanwhile, as soon as they see the darkness of night thinning
with the light now near, when the dawn, going before,
announces the sun, scattering the redness it has received
and veiling the wandering stars with saffron dye,
they vie to bring the man, seized, to the cell of holy
Martin, so that at last, the cloud scattered, put to flight,
the demon might lose the fictions of his deceitful wit,
betraying the fraud exposed before so great a judge.
But he, resisting, as the danger now drew nearer,
strove to refuse and escape the holy hands of those seizing him,
halting his step and resisting with his voice,
crying that he was forbidden to approach the cell of holy
Martin and to bring that garment forth over the threshold.
Then indeed they press on: fear betrays the fraud
and pale cowardice lays bare the contrived deceits.
The image of the garment vanished in the hands of those holding it,
and the appearance slipped away and left their intent eyes:
as fleeces of mist with airy threads,
which have covered hollow valleys with a counterfeit flood,
when the bright sun raises his pure orb higher,
lay bare the plains as the darkness is scattered.
This trophy too, holy Martin, fix to the cross,
by which you strip the cruel tyrant of his feigned garment,
tearing the lying coverings of an airy web
and scattering the floating fleeces of a hollow cloud.
O fury never to cease, do you rise again,
crushed so often? So often losing your efforts,
you rush in and fall, and your audacity sets no end,
nor does success achieve your wish? Do you, impious one, counterfeit
the face of the Lord, and with darkness to deceive the light
do you try, so that with such an appearance the saint
your senseless madness might delude by contrived forms,
breathing out your last venom, though without wounding,
and blowing out an exhausted rage from now empty jaws?
You do not penetrate a pure mind with foul gloom,
nor do the shadows of mists shut out the true sun;
and though, radiant with purple and flashing with gems,
you placed ruddy gold beneath your lying feet,
counterfeiting the true king with a false diadem,
crying out, oh grief, that you, faithless one, were the eternal Christ,
so that, veiled under a holy name, there might perhaps lie hidden
an impiety that feigned God, meaning to persuade the blessed man
to trust the enemy under the lying appearance of deity
and to bend his holy limbs in honour of a demon,
so that a religion wrongly believed, alas the outrage, might make the saint sacrilegious
and he might lose the merits of faith by believing,
and the deceitful cups of poison, wickedly to be offered,
might hide the dire juice with the sweetness of honey.
Lay these out for ignorant minds; for recruits these
ambushes contrive, men who do not yet
attempt to rehearse the trumpets of war with untried weapons.
But he who is accustomed to sweat under arms no longer raw,
and to enclose the auspicious standards with a rampart thrown before them,
who hides his veteran grey hairs under a venerable helmet,
who, taught by long practice, has foreseen all things,
carefully exploring which places are secure for laying
ambushes, or which in turn are suspect and to be guarded against,
with what skill to direct the shield, with what whirl the spear,
what honours win the king, what charges do harm:
he will resist all ambushes with such constant gravity
and will guard against deceits with such reasoning
that the enemy, broken in combat, cannot achieve by fraud
what he cannot by valour. Flourishing with such strength then
was Martin as a warrior, when the trumpets of Christ
were utterly overturning the crimes of a corrupted world.
He knew how to discern the sign of his king
and to trample such pomps in the name of the Crucified.
You now feign Christ in a purple mantle
and with gold and gems; with the foreign thread of the Seres
you adorn this appearance, wretch, alas, and do not know how to deceive.
So, losing the so often frustrated efforts of your
scheme, slipping away again into the thin air,
you are dissolved, and confess your flight with a foul stench.
But you, firm in unmoved virtue, triumph,
saint of God, to whom you cling with perpetual virtue.
You strengthened, unconquered against all crimes, your conduct,
gentle, patient, just, pious, upright, fair,
mild, confident, humble, kind without gall,
learned, courteous, approachable, easily appeased, keen,
holy bishop, good teacher, lovable host,
to be wondered at for signs, likewise to be imitated for conduct,
humble in heart, excellent in mind, venerable in both,
while by fleeing praise you gain it, by avoiding it you deserve it,
drawing out successive days into late fasts
and, always most sparing, with scarcely even meagre food
relieving your weary stomach without the weight of meat.
So the pleasure of food was driven out, so that of sleep cast off,
lest this earthly burden weigh on the wakeful mind,
but that the body might grow used to the light rule of the soul,
keeping watch in zeal for praying and zeal for reading.
His time clung continuously to these cares;
this alone pleased [him] as rest: to change one labour
for another succeeding it, the unbroken [labour] of prayer without end.
Let us all also marvel, rejoicing, that nature itself
yielded to so great a man. Though the lowest
cleric, forgetful of so great an honour, had wronged him,
he did not, wronged, swell with gall, nor ever by a judge's
right burn with love of vengeance against those subject to him.
Fury did not stir hatred, nor joys laughter,
nor grief sadness. Holy in venerable gravity,
an angelic countenance shone in his venerable body,
which could express the face of his holy heart
and bring forth the light shut within his sacred breast.
Always God on his lips, always compassion. Peace
he kept in counsel and in desire. For often
envy used to arm jaws infected with the livid venom
with reproaches, and to inflame with dire
gall even the bishops, so that they preferred to carp with their tongues
than to equal the holy man in deeds. Not even so
did anger drive the saint's mind even to wish for requital.
Rather, for so great an offence he shed brotherly tears;
his gentle compassion poured them forth with wet face,
beseeching the Lord Christ with a river of tears
to spare those deceitful words by granting pardon.
So, with a heart always steady against every wound,
rage roused no hatred in him; rather, the cause roused grief:
like the martyr who, following the footsteps of the Lord,
taking the cruel downpour from a cloud of stones,
as he breathed out his faint life from his blessed breast,
asked that their crimes be forgiven the frenzied mob,
grieving more for the sins of the people than for the wounds of his flesh.
BOOK FOUR.
The translation I had begun had finished the volume I took up,
running through the pure copies of the holy book,
when suddenly the glory of a hidden
story was offered to us, spurring on the efforts of our wish:
not so that what the page of so clear-sighted a heart had marked
might shine out better from my wretched mouth,
since the force of words, flashing with living power,
would lose its inborn vigour once softened into metre.
But because not all seek out the inner recesses of a clear spring
to be searched more deeply, a great part
often drinks from the open streams nearer at hand, neglecting the coolness,
we too, who can produce nothing worthy of the learned,
will hold out cloudy cups to the idle not far off.
Often, too, the whistles sent out from a twisted reed
try to equal the voices of blaring trumpets,
and he who is used to resting beneath a lofty pine
at times makes his way into the thickets of a cheap willow-bed.
You too, who prefer to come into pleasing groves,
if perhaps the road to a far-removed wood wearies you,
hurry and break into the thicket offered close at hand.
The saint was going to the threshold of the blessed church,
to bring the accustomed mysteries to eternal Christ.
But look, a poor man, trembling with icy cold,
knocking his wretched teeth together with nodding head
and fitting his raised hands to his pale cheeks,
was trying to catch a faint warmth with his breath.
An icicle, congealing, hardened his frequent tears.
His voice too, sounding tearfully in broken words,
cut short by weeping sounds and speaking with a groan,
made his whole complaint plain, his plight crying out.
These things might perhaps have softened a hard sternness:
much less could Martin's well-known kindness
ignore the distress of this wretched, wailing man.
At once he orders the deacon standing by, whom,
in the manner of his predecessors, the bishop had chosen as keeper of the holy chest,
to buy a garment at the Lord's cost and with [His] money
and hurry to fit it on the freezing body.
So he left what he wanted done as if done,
then, entering the dwelling of his secluded cell,
which here too used to separate the saint from the nearby crowds
when he was about to go forth to the sacred mysteries,
receiving the monk, and soon to send out the minister.
But where would the wretched not make their way, whom distress forces
to lay bare the exposed shame of a worn-out face?
What was not open even to priests, need broke into,
pleading its plaintive case, since the gift had been delayed.
Then pity truly seized his whole mind,
and he did not wish to risk the command again.
He covered his head with his *amphibalus* [cloak]. Then, with the witness away,
he drew back his bent arms little by little toward his limbs,
shaking off the gathered garment from his bent-over chest.
Nor was his body seen naked once the poor man was clothed:
so quickly did his outer wrap cover the despoiled man
that, anticipating the wish of the hurrying poor man, it left
the man himself unaware of the deed, whom he had made glad
with the gift, hidden from the witness, plain to the needy.
Tell me, you who, trampling the joys of a scorned world,
have chosen to seek life by casting away your wealth:
who, stripping himself, has covered the naked with his own cloak?
Who has not shunned for himself what he grieved that another bore?
Who, willing to be wretched, has restored the wretched by pitying?
You have surpassed the examples of the men of old, Martin,
and yourself. You were admirable then, when the poor man was covered,
since at least a portion of the divided garment remained.
Yield to yourself! By this gift you have doubled your old palm.
Meanwhile, as was the custom, the deacon reminds [him] that it is the hour
for the solemn rites to be performed in the assembly of the people.
He says: 'The teaching of the holy prophet must be fulfilled.
Let mercy precede the mass. This is the more pleasing
offering. Doing the command, first cover the naked man.'
Going out a little and looking for the poor man, he
reports in turn that he is gone and not to be found for the gift.
'Come, bring out the gift,' said the saint, 'a needy man will not be lacking.'
Then a garment bought for barely an eighth of a *solidus*,
woven of knotty threads from bristly fleece,
he throws down, vexed, before the saint's feet.
With the deacon moved a little away, he squeezes his precious
limbs, rejoicing, hastily into so cheap a covering.
So the hero goes to the altar far more finely adorned
in this dress, like a soldier who, when the king returns after wars,
runs to meet him wet with sweat and dust,
the more handsome in his honours the more unsightly in limbs and face.
For the work of virtue surpasses its appearance, as the strength
of a deep root outlasts the seasons of the leaves.
And no doubtful conjecture soon proved this wish [approved].
For while he heaped up the holy gifts with the solemn prayer
and accompanied the immortal vows with sacred words,
a glowing flame shone out from his bright head,
pouring splendour over his head, harmless to his hair,
stretched upward and raised in a clear trail,
breaking through the liquid air with a fire-streaming furrow.
Go on, then, Glory, driven by the continuous whirl of his titles,
so stirred by the easy course of his miracles
that, running with reins fully slack into joys,
you take up what is to be begun before you leave what is closed.
There was a certain rich man, Evanthius, and, although
bound to the cares of this world by tenacious chains,
yet of unharmed faith and kindly heart,
keeping his mind pure from earthly crime.
His marrow wholly eaten away by violent fever,
shaking his trembling inwards with frequent breaths
and breaking out in sighs with a sobbing pulse,
a suppliant, with the confused murmur of a parched tongue,
and the plectrum of his voice hindered by the glue
of a dried palate, often striving with broken speech
to make his feeling known, he asks that the pitiable entreaty
of those praying obtain the saint's coming to him quickly,
and that, if anyone be spurred either by care for his pain
or by love of kindness, seeking remedies for his health,
he go to this man alone: for the restoring of his life's span
the sight of Martin surpassed all cures.
Nor does even a delay slow the just wish.
He believed that, for the wished-for signs by divine gift,
this faith was enough. And soon the fact itself proved it.
Scarcely had part of even half the journey been covered
(a great part of the road remained) when grace forestalled
him as he went. Power, swifter than his slow limbs,
going ahead, sent on before the gifts of the hoped-for health.
The man, well again, ran to meet the physician. Both rejoice,
the body healed, at the health poured over into their hearts,
while through the merits of faith the curing of the flesh grows.
So when the cause of all delays had been removed,
though wishing to return at once, overcome by many prayers
he granted the space of one day, as they begged.
But what had been short in space is ample in miracles:
work not narrow makes up for narrow time.
For a boy, whom an evil serpent had by chance struck
with a deadly bite, infected with the gall of poison,
when the venom was already swelling his livid limbs,
and the serpent's raging bane, drunk deep even into
his very vitals, as if death were accomplished,
was loosing his fading eyes in an infernal sleep,
his master himself, bending his loyal back to a just labour,
carried to the holy feet of the true patron,
not doubting, from merits proved by so many proofs,
that being present he could drive out the venom by touch,
who by coming had put diseases to flight by terror alone.
Without delay the healing of his right hand, touching the wound,
cleansed the chilled limbs of the foul poison:
and wherever the holy hand ran over the body,
death fled, and life returned. The plague, gathered,
soon went back to a single place. Then in the wound alone
he packed the venom, bidden at once to burst out,
and the boy, steadying his steps with fearless effort,
ran with unafraid strides as his master rejoiced.
With this reward you return rich, these gifts you take,
counting the happy gifts of health added besides.
What time was empty of miracles even on the highroad itself?
What road did not seek heaven, though a guest on earth?
The shepherd was going round the folds of the flock entrusted to him,
in which the holy Church enclosed the country people,
lest perhaps the tricks of thieves or the fury of wolves
should snatch away the unwary sheep when the guard was away.
Meanwhile, having perhaps left his companions a little behind,
he was going on ahead along the way, where the public highroad
stretches its raised mass across the level plains,
so that the road, made firm and raised with paving stones,
might tip the poured-out rains into the hollows below,
and the heavy rut not sink into the hard track,
and the muddy depth not swallow wagons sunk in it,
but the whirl of wheels might barely graze the back of the road's top,
marking its traces with no furrow,
but betraying [them] far off by the ringing of the striking iron.
Along this road Martin was going, a little ahead,
when suddenly he saw coming toward him a carriage hurrying
in a great whirlwind, which happened to be carrying men puffed up
with the terror of military office. No order could calm their fury,
no reason their crazed minds.
Ambition, drunkenness, shouting, frenzy, anger, uproar
stirred their disordered breasts with various monsters,
and among the breathless mules and the frightened drivers
rang out the blows of those striking, the words of those shouting.
There was no rule of stopping, nor did care for danger
slow their swift course over the level, over the steep.
So, different from such men in dress and face,
the saint came to meet them. The beasts feared the venerable
face of the man before them. The mules, trembling, gave way
from the middle of the road, with sounder heart [than their masters],
their trembling bodies bound in tangled reins:
as once, the reading tells, the she-ass, when [her master] was forbidden to curse the holy people,
scorned her profane master,
crushing his foot, pressing it with her leaning body.
Then, their hearts flooded with mad poison,
they leap down. They have hope of their wish, a cause given for raging:
they even dared to stretch out sacrilegious right hands against the saint
and to batter with blows, vying with one another, the holy body,
innocent, alone, gentle, calm, enduring.
Angry, unsteady, many, swollen, frenzied,
they drive, hold, and batter him as he met the blows
and uttered not a word at all. His face grows wet
with blood, his breath bursts from his bruised chest,
his livid jaws grow black with crushed throat,
and his failing eyes, by the light of Christ alone,
weigh the present darkness. His sight fails in the gloom
of night, but hope shines in his breast.
So when his companions saw their master in such a state,
the band turned pale, half-dead at the sight of their patron,
stretching out humble hands to hold him up
and pressing tender kisses on his bloodied limbs.
Then they hurry to leave the grim scene of the dreadful beating.
A little donkey took the venerable weight upon its back,
to carry its accustomed load. But with his body bent,
the half-alive burden sways, his limbs slumped over,
and threatens an uncertain fall, on the point of slipping off.
Meanwhile, their rage spent and their hearts sated,
the men returned to the carriage. Then they force
the beasts to burst away swiftly in a headlong leap,
so that whatever delay there had been in the murderous beating
they might at once make up by the whirl of a rapid course.
But they make these efforts in vain. The beasts stand fixed
and defy the savage command. The mules, bound
by the Lord's decision, stiffened into the likeness of statues.
Then indeed their anger burns worse, in mad uproar.
Shouts are of no use, whips of no use. Their bruised flanks
ring back. They snatch from the nearby woods [material] for blows.
Stones, stakes, cudgels, goads, whatever each found
as he searched and anger made a weapon, he spends on strokes.
Yet these cannot loosen the stiffened sinews
or move the fixed limbs. You would think
cold bronze or figures carved in stone had stiffened there.
At last, when their fury was wholly spent and broken,
their senseless madness admitted sound understanding,
so that they knew the mules, tied fast amid so many blows,
were numbed by God's judgement, and that the cause of the delay
befell the wretches not without a divine nod.
Then at last, stunned by the portent and with their fury laid aside,
mindful of their sin they ask who that man was who on his venerable
body had received the sacrilegious blows of their beating.
And see, when they heard Martin's name, they come running
and fall prostrate, their torn hair fouled with dust,
and, watering their streaming cheeks with a fountain of tears,
they humbly twine their arms about his blessed feet,
asking pardon and at the same time confessing their guilt.
Nor indeed was the pitiable entreaty of those begging
put off for long: mercy cut short their prolonged weeping,
and the gift of pardon came before the prayers of those asking.
Without delay the freedom to depart was restored: with a quick
word he loosened the reins of the delay he had commanded.
Tell me, what can the swift carriage of your king
accomplish when God holds it back? Compare brows flashing
with the rays of gems, and coverings bristling
with goat-hair, the titles of power and the pomp of those who give orders, with miracles.
Then at least, taught by the weight of the saint's merits,
rank his command as better than that of your king.
Come, go on, my Muse, my priest, and in a continuous course
relate in song the lineage of his miracles, the history,
and my talent. Touch the plectrum of my heart or mouth
with your aid. Let madmen speaking frenzy
snatch the Muses to their raving breasts:
let Martin drive us. Such a change of mind
is welcome to me; my inmost being thirsts for such a fountain.
Let crazed breasts ask for Castalian waters:
other cups befit men reborn in the Jordan.
Again the saint was making his venerable journey on foot,
where the walls of the Carnutes lie amid open plains.
So here, while he passed through the byways of the fertile countryside,
just wonder filled the neighbouring village.
Countless people gather from all sides; every sex and age
is there. The great glory of the man strips the fields,
emptied of their tillers. Care for their homes is now less.
To have seen Martin is enough. At this name even the
pagans themselves rightly stood amazed, as at a title of praise,
and although they had not yet received the power of the faith,
they streamed in haste to the fame of so great a master.
A dense throng of country people crowded close:
just wonder had covered the open plains.
What fruit from the sowing of so great a harvest of salvation
you would eagerly rejoice to store in the barns entrusted to you,
looking back at stalks emptied of the weight of their grain!
When suddenly a mother appears, clasping the lifeless body
of her son, beating the empty jaws against her breast
and plunging her plaintive breast into the icy lips,
pleading with trembling words amid her sighs
and watering her pale cheeks with a river of tears.
His mind, full of God, sensed the gifts of a favouring God
close at hand. Grace quickened his pure understanding,
so that he trusted that so great a crowd would be called to the divine rewards,
at least once they had seen the power of the Lord.
So when the suppliant mother laid the pitiable corpse
of her dead son in his blessed arms,
the limbs, once touched, began to move; the eyes opened
and lay unclosed, and gradually grew used to the light pouring in;
and the tongue, striking the plectrum against the moist palate,
shaped into words the voice forced from the throat:
and, joyfully hanging its arms clasped round his neck,
the child, neglecting his mother, asked for Martin's embrace.
Open wide your spreading bosom, enriched by the peoples received,
and joyfully embrace the people added to you,
bride of God, drawing the whole world into your heart.
But you idols, long stinking in wretched tombs,
mourn at last the triumphs that are a cause for joy.
What hearts did not yield to you, holy one, as you taught?
What wildness was not tamed? Since always, even in
kings themselves, the hardness set against your prayers
the forerunning mercy of Christ the Lord would soften.
But fiercer than the rest, and terrible through the vice of pride and anger,
Valentinian held the throne;
and when Martin often approached that ruler as a suppliant,
pleading a difficult case under a harsh prince,
the king, offended by the petitioner's so constant entreaty,
so that he should not often batter his blocked ears with complaints,
orders the saint to be kept from the doors. Rebuffed,
he leaves the turbulent inner halls of the hostile king,
preferring to knock at the threshold of eternal Christ
and to enter that court which gives to kings themselves
their right, enclosing their times within fixed bounds,
though it restrains their stiff mouths with strong reins.
So his whole mind returns to its accustomed rigour,
afflicting the thin flesh on his wearied body,
goading his wasted skin with a covering of hair,
passing the day in fasting, the darkness in watching,
and joining both times together with continuous weeping.
And if ever his eyes gave way to brief sleep,
the bare ground laid beneath him was enough for his light slumber,
until Christ, pitying the sorrow of his holy disciple,
sent comfort to his afflicted friend,
brought in a kindly address. For an angel of the Lord, gliding from on high,
speaks these words of the command:
'Come, go on, and enter the blocked hall without fear.
Nothing is shut when God has mercy. To one for whom the palace of heaven
has opened as he prayed, these earthly barriers will open.'
Without delay, with so great a guarantor, his faith in the divine favour
was sure. Fearless, he makes for the tyrant's threshold, to pass
within. The guard of the swollen-proud king gave way,
and the arms set at the watch with dire threats.
When the king suddenly saw him from his lofty throne,
he was dumbfounded, stunned by the sight, and fiercely
glared from the royal seat at his trembling, threatening attendants.
Meanwhile, to take comfort in slighting the saint,
deigning no honour to him as he stood close by,
he kept his seat beneath him with unmoving limbs.
But see, in a rapid whirl of crackling flame,
a fierce avenging fire, sent by divine gift,
enveloped the king's throne and part of the one seated.
Then at last, leaving the blaze with a quick leap,
he planted his steps, trembling, his limbs shaken,
glad to render to the holy man the honour wrung from him,
and with kindly affection to remove the cause of his petition,
submitting his harsh heart to the saint's precepts
and bending his ways, now teachable, to his commanding words.
Then too he heaped on him quite lavish gifts with royal
provision. But a mind rich in God wished to take nothing
from the wealth of the world, leaving earthly
rewards and storing up instead the gifts of eternal Christ.
Now, since my poorest songs, in common words,
have burst into lofty palaces in humble verse,
we shall speak, in continuous discourse, as Christ grants,
of the heights of kings made subject to the merits of the saints.
After, as the page of the book already gone through recorded,
Maximus cleansed the crimes of the reign he had assumed,
he prudently strove to keep the favour he had begun to win
by constant attentions. For he delighted to summon
the saint in this way, desiring from the river of the divine word
to give his faith water to drink, and from the fountain of the blessed
mouth to draw the nectar-sweet liquor of doctrine,
to learn the titles of the saints and the deeds of the pious,
what battles they toiled in as they fought, or what
rewards they won as victors, what glory awaits
the just, what punishment the guilty, how the Father's mercy
cherishes, how heavily the sentence of the King strikes.
The saint, rejoicing with him as he asked such things, [was glad] to set forth each one
and to call back the light, the darkness driven out.
But the queen, not inferior to so great a husband,
outdid the devoted king in diligent services.
Always hanging on the holy mouth of the speaker,
and close by sprinkling his feet with abundant weeping,
she equalled the merit of her who with her blessed hair
wiped the Lord's feet, first washed with tears.
But she thinks these things small, and, girded apart for a special
service, prepares to serve him with affection, so that alone, the servants
removed, the happy queen might set the table.
Nor did she cease from her prayers, often pressing her suit
with her husband joined to her, until by continual weeping
and constant entreaty she compelled the saint to yield.
She sets the table, places the chair, offers of her own accord
towels for drying hands and water for washing them,
and the food she had cooked, rejoicing in her service,
she herself hurries to bring in conspicuous baskets.
And for as long as she, never wearied, had been free from serving,
she filled up the constant toil by the virtue of standing,
as the venerable reward for so great a work
gathering fragments of the crumbs, so that the food of faith,
precious by his touch, might satisfy her holy hunger.
O happy woman, by your virtue preferring these
treasures to royal wealth, preferring to serve the blessed man
rather than to excel wholly in the whole world,
transferring the honour of a reigning queen to the name of a handmaid.
Temples radiant with star-like gems did not
change your mind, nor silks stiff with gleaming threads,
nor gold more precious for purple woven into it.
By the merit of so great a faith, queen, you equalled
her who, lofty in the honour of a like throne,
came from the ends of the earth to come to know Solomon,
and, journeying far, sought what she held within herself.
You bring out the riches of your heart for love of the wise word,
catching by hearing what you may retain with a teachable mind.
Such as you were, you trod down the obstacles of the world beneath you,
a woman made equal to the glories of men of old.
For often kings unconquered in many a contest
were overcome by deadly pride alone, refusing the yoke.
Rightly, then, you received a special gift from the saint,
that for you, his sternness a little softened and laid aside,
the gentle secrets of his heavenly heart should lie open.
How many waves has a holy brow, though relaxed to only a slight calm,
mercifully bidden to settle!
How many storms has a milder breeze stilled,
and a clear sky, though it shines only briefly among the clouds!
How many sad defendants has this table released, what chains
has a little freedom permitted loosed, and how many fetters
has a brief hour shaken off, relaxing its own sternness!
For time, person and place stand beside the counsels
of the wise, and guide the mind by a reason suited to the moment.
Do not hold up to me the name of the female sex,
envious one: not limbs but hearts will win merit.
Nor is human nature less, when grace is equal;
nor do race, sex and age differ in the merit of faith,
man or woman, slave or free, foreigner or heir.
It is the believer's merit that excels, not the glory of the flesh.
Next, what I have learned this sex has earned by faithful zeal,
wishing to touch on it with brief signs,
I will recount in whatever words Christ shall give.
While the saint, going forward, was making his venerable journey,
as day was turning to night he made for a nearby
dwelling, and, received under the roof of a rejoicing village,
he hurried to seek out the inner sanctuary of the holy church.
And here, as always, a guest of the blessed threshold,
he allowed his weary body to rest a little,
relaxing his drooping eyes in a brief sleep,
so that, renewed by even a short and modest slumber,
his very thin limbs might suffice for unceasing labour
and, through this support, bear up his watchful mind.
But when the light, shining out of the night, had passed through the darkness,
having swiftly and solemnly performed all his duties
he hurried on his way again. Then indeed a faithful
band of girls, whom holy virginity had consecrated to the Lord,
untouched in flesh and chaste in heart,
so that the frail corruption of the flesh should not press down to earth
a mind hastening to the heights of heaven,
burst rejoicing into the inner room of the holy cell,
blessed by his holy lodging there, and their breath drinks in
the fresh air and absorbs the air he had imbued.
Then in humble reverence they venerate the teacher's seat
and hastily mark with kisses each single place
which the feet of him standing had touched, which the limbs of him lying,
which had been blessed by his holy food, which pressed by his seat,
or which had lain beneath his prostrate limbs as he prayed.
But when, having seen the straw of his blessed bed,
they felt the hay warmed by his holy body,
a violent modesty contends for the booty found,
while each seizes a share for herself, and, their bosoms filled,
the packed stalks prick their tender breasts,
and their thin garments keep them off their prickled breasts.
What may true faith not do? By chance one of the company
of virgins, no less chaste in heart than in body,
when a demon, holding some poor wretch by violent right,
was forcing him to break out into commanded frenzies,
shaking sound sense out of his captive breast,
trusting in God's help and in the merit of her patron,
wisely lavish with a little piece of the booty she had seized,
ties it round the wretch's throat and hangs
on the raving man's neck the hay pressed by the blessed body.
Without delay, at the touch, the enemy, at once terrified,
fled the dry stalks as if they were fierce fire,
no match for the straws that Martin's body had touched.
And yet, crushed so often and so often put to flight,
you dare, madman, to come against him in changed forms,
to try a man you had tested, and before his face to bear
his awe-inspiring eyes, and, hiding your appearance, to display your fury.
For, sitting on the back of a beast and shaking with frenzies
the butting animal, and plunging into its entrails,
with deadly rage he had driven out the beast's nature.
Or when you pressed the back of a captive heifer,
so that she carried the monster set upon her, not merely in body,
fulfilling the frenzy poured through her possessed limbs
and fitting her service to the motions of the raging one,
scattering a bloody dew from her shaken head,
while red drops run over her smooth temples
and fiery horns go before her angry brow,
and her quick breath hardly blows out the alternating air,
and she raises a cloud of dust with bent hock,
and her trembling foot scatters fine sand upward.
Indeed, having raged everywhere among the fleeing crowds,
at the sight of the saint, her rider driven off, she grew gentle
and stood still, and, her burden thrown off but her mind recovered,
the young cow joyfully rejoined the herds of her companions.
Now at least stop plunging into the flocks of Christ,
since the saint has not left you rights even over beasts.
We yield: the glory of his powers surpasses the faltering words
of the speaker, more shown forth by illustrious deeds
than to be set out by the sounds of the tongue. Let poets
bring obscure things to light by speaking: we are overcome
by the light of praise, and, overwhelmed by such splendour, lie hidden.
And would that the glory of so illustrious a patron, when touched,
might make our night grow a little thinner,
so that we do not cover the light of the story with a darkened heart
and the sins of the speaker do not lessen the title of his praise.
What heart was not calm toward the saint, what anger rebellious,
what fierceness not gentle? The Molossian hounds felt
his command, when wanton youths in the hunt were pounding
the level stretches of open fields as they crossed them,
taking slopes down or up with a swift leap.
The hurrying horses were wet with much sweat
and breathed out thin air from wide nostrils.
The roused hoof resounded with a terrifying beat,
leaving a cloud of dust behind its swift tracks.
Nor was the swift running of the winged horses enough:
the riders' hanging chests were so level with the horses' forward-thrust heads
that the slowness of the steeds delayed the wishes of those seated,
and the motion of the drivers outran the running of the carriers.
The eager Molossians strove to equal the winds,
and in their zeal to win to satisfy the frenzy of the onlookers,
and their trembling open jaws shook, with alternate breaths,
their tongues hanging far out from their gaping throats.
This great toil, this expense—where, alas, does it end?
What fruit or what use is there in catching fleeing
little beasts and rejoicing in the flight of frightened hares?
You, Martin, wisely despised such madness,
pitying the sad fate of an innocent creature, and made the gaping
mouths of the dogs and their hurried steps grow numb.
Now if by chance he had relaxed his close sternness,
with what salt of words he used to dispel the cares of his companions
and refresh their attentive ears a little,
shrewd with gravity, witty with religion,
sprinkling the virtue of his heart with the flower of charm.
Seeing a swineherd covered in a garment of skins,
he said: 'Look, another Adam! Such clothing veiled
the first parent when stripped, wrapping his shivering limbs
and giving small comfort to his new shame,
when, after the deadly venom of the poison of Tartarus,
his deceived body felt the slippery hissings.
But as for us, stripped utterly and utterly buried
to the old sin, may new grace clothe us again.'
Likewise, he saw a sheep, its wool stripped off from its shorn fleece,
and smiled at it. Then at once from there,
taking in order from the deed examples for teaching:
'See, the humble sheep has fulfilled the commandment.
Of two garments it gave one to him who asked,
unwilling to keep the first while another grows in its place.
But how shameful it is for us to have been outdone by a brute beast,
if, lavish, it surpasses us with more bountiful giving.'
But on the other side lay open the ridges of meadows,
marked out in differing state. One part had suffered
being rooted up by greedy swine, and its ridges,
black with upturned clods, had lost their green colour.
But another, shorn with its turf gnawed bare and dismal,
the herds had stripped in their hunger, and the mouths of oxen,
eating face down, had taken away the garment of the glad earth,
while the dewy grasses are cropped with wide bite,
drawn to the jaws by the roughness of the curved tongue,
which, going first and licking, gathers the tender plants,
so that the greedy teeth may cut the packed fodder.
No less had the hoof, its horn pressed down, trodden it away,
crushing the green shoots with frequent stamping.
Another part, of an unharmed field green with fresh turf,
nature adorned, dressing it with varied beauty.
The green grasses waved in the light breeze,
and a gentle wind moved the plants it stirred.
Besides, countless flowers over the lying plains
painted the level ground, set off with inset gems.
Some, purple tinged and dyed with a rosy hue,
while others shone, distinguished by snowy whiteness,
and among them, marking the grasses with saffron signs,
the golden grace of yellow flowers glowed red-gold.
Purple drops bend the gem-like shoots,
and amber beads of moist dew bowed the plants.
A sweet scent, striving to equal the pleasing colour,
blending harmonious joys in equal forms,
fed the sight with beauty, the nostrils with fragrance.
Scattered leaves gave very pleasant shade,
and dark-green arms nodded with interwoven branches.
Birds hidden in the leaves strove in spring song,
modulating musical whistles with sweet-sounding tongues.
A clear stream fed the nearby plants
and, grazing the grasses, nourished them with gliding moisture.
Beneath, transparent pebbles, as the gaze pierced through,
rippled the glassy waters with gentle obstacles,
nor could the beauty, though submerged, be taken from the eyes,
a sight open to vision even though covered by the stream.
Why do I try to mark out these forms in rough speech?
These things cannot be expressed in words, which, by Christ's gift,
the grace of nature has portrayed and painted better.
So, seeing this scene marked out in unlike forms,
Martin said: 'Compare for a moment
the separate parts of the meadow—grazed, dug up, unharmed—
with the crime of harlots, with wives wedded
in lawful union, or with virgins who vow
holy bodies to Christ, adorned with the gems of rosy modesty.
As there, in the rooted-up field, beauty does not remain,
so the image of Christ, smeared with vices, does not shine.
As here the root remains safe, though the grass is cut,
so for the married their faith is secure, without the flower of chastity.
As colour and brightness smile in the flowering field,
so the glory of pure flesh will shine bright.'
As he was giving such lessons of clear strength
and of a heart ever intent on divine rewards,
a certain man approached, a monk, who had gained this name by abandoning
military service, and who, after the trumpets and bugles of war,
had preferred to give himself to the standards of the true King,
following instead the great banners of the holy cross.
Indeed, drawing the partner of his marriage-bed into a shared way of life,
he had directed her to be a companion to the holy
virgins, giving up the rights of the marriage-bed and of the flesh.
But when wanton pleasure, revived once more,
began to goad his mind and deep into his marrow
to instil the mortal joys of the world he had scorned,
wishing to loosen the rigour he had barely tasted,
running back again to the embraces and desires of the married,
[and], after the titles of a monk, to take up again the name of husband,
he even set about assailing his teacher with frequent clamour,
mixing such complaints with his prayers:
'If Christ grants me the comforts of marriage,
having deigned to join the opposite sex in the marriage-bed,
who will snatch from me the gifts of God? Who by a new law
will dare to tear up the ancient law of the Lord?'
As he broke out in such mutterings with headlong mind,
the healing art of the holy patron approached him more gently:
'Come, tell me, if you recall the times of your past life,
whether you fought the savage enemy in pitched battle.
And since you remember that this happened very often, likewise
consider whether, amid the clarions and war-trumpets,
and the javelins poised by the terrifying arms of the fighters,
and the drawn swords, and the silken [standards], swollen with the wind they catch,
imitating the coils or the fury of serpents,
the female sex ever disgraced the battle-lines.
What place is there for wool-baskets among shields, for girls among arms?
Did a sprinkling of dust ever become smooth faces?
But if these things are not fitting for earthly camps,
that anything womanly should suit the standards of men,
then for you, who wage war in close-pressed sweat,
will not the mingling of the renounced sex be more shameful still?
In a time of idleness let wanton pleasure
find such a laughable troupe. But when the lines of men
hasten into the fields and the iron-clad
columns gleam, let walls defend the crowds of women,
and, distrusting arms, let them strive to shut themselves in behind gates.
But he who hastens to war, let him scorn comforts.'
With such words he healed the wounds of the unbridled mind,
and gave new joys again to the calmed heart,
and sent the fighting man back to the wars in peace.
Now who could worthily recount this:
how great a patience adorned so teachable a grace?
It happened that among girls holy in both heart and body,
ever flourishing, precious in perpetual chastity,
whom unwed virginity, devoted to Christ, had joined to the Lord
by a bond of the mind, not by a covenant of the flesh,
one had surpassed them all in zeal for the virtues,
adding this special glory to the honours of chastity,
that, once withdrawn from the eyes of all men,
she kept the rigour she had begun with a steadfast heart,
nor did she waver, a light woman of unstable mind,
overcoming by the weight of virtue her inborn sex
and the scarce and rare examples of the men before her.
Just admiration for this resolve drove the saint
to visit such a girl, rightly honouring her,
drawn by so great a flower of virtues.
But so steadfastly fixed in her breast remained
her faith, now devoted to the Lord, that the barriers of chastity,
closed to men, preserving the honours of a glorious palm,
not even the merit of so great a patron could unlock.
Yet his faith, rejoicing in her resolve, did not blush
to bear the welcome refusal; but he, kindly,
counted as his own honour all that had given him hope,
attending more to the gains of the soul than to the joys of the flesh.
What part will you snatch for yourself, what part from that holy breast,
Ambition, puffed up by the winds of mad swelling?
Lie now utterly cast down. Christ can have nothing
in common with vices. Those who swell with praise
desire to be exalted. He shows clearly enough,
who desires to stay hidden and scorns the heights of the world,
how he gives to the Lord alone the honour that he avoids.
But you, who would rather be held cheap so that Christ be praised,
adding this judgement too to your blessed honours,
the praise you flee by avoiding it, by avoiding it you earn.
BOOK FIVE.
Once already brought forth in praise of so great a patron,
why, tongue, are you silent, shutting the rough mutterings of your voice
and untaught sounds away in long silences?
If it is shameful to speak of such great things, this law for modesty
should have been laid down earlier. Too late
you try to hold these veils before a brow too worn.
But if you are held by the base torpor of idleness,
so that the grim image of foul death may depart,
shake off the languid sleep from your weighed-down breast,
that, wakeful, with death shaken off, you may rise again to Christ.
If you lie cast down deservedly, trust in the patron.
Why do you tremble as one guilty and due punishment, when you are one bound by a vow?
Come then, and commit the quenched ember to the Lord,
that the stiffness of my wit may grow warm as Christ breathes upon it,
and Martin's prayer may melt the ice of my heart
and make a dumb voice break forth at once,
as once it won the miracle of a like deed.
Where the walls of the Carnutes lie in open plains,
and Gaul stretches far and wide in boundless fields,
here a daughter, who had been silent, mute, for twelve years,
and, her mouth blocked, had unlocked it for no speech,
the saddest care of grieving parents,
increased the wretched pair's constant grief by living,
and with the span of years the wounds of mourning grew.
Alas, how often they grieved that the gifts of mighty God,
granted to others, were lost to them, when they often saw
children scarcely crawling break out into words,
and names come out broken from tender little lips,
when loving devotion, running ahead, marked the uncertain murmur,
recognising the unclear voice with affection as interpreter,
taking up sounds as if they were words and seizing on what was about to be said.
These things, which are granted to others after the first cradle,
their envious love had wept for through twelve years,
while, grieving through two lustra and two years,
it longed for a first word by the time of marriageable age:
until, clasping and clinging to Martin's knees,
the father, half-dead, weeping with tearful face,
set out his whole complaint as his groans laid it open,
drawing sighs pulled up from the depths of his breast,
breaking his tearful murmur with frequent sobs,
and drenching his wet breast with the rain from his cheeks.
And already love of his accustomed compassion had stirred
Martin's kindly mind. But the cause of delay
came from his integrity, care for precious modesty,
and the restraint that must always accompany famous deeds,
lest boasting lose the merit a deed had conferred
and presumption of heart spoil the work of power.
So he said: 'Unworthy for the miracle of so great a deed
I think myself, and with trembling neck I dread a weight
which in my weakness I cannot bear, lest a greater burden
press me down and, feeble, I labour under too heavy a load.
But no cure whatever is difficult for Christ,
who rightly entrusts these signs to other ministers,
so that the Lord's miracles may reveal the merit of the saints.
See, two men stand by, famous for integrity and faith
and power, whom such a life has rightly raised
to this office. Will not the Lord's healing more readily
grant to them these things, which, being great, exceed our
merit, but are not hard for saints?'
Often repeating such proofs of a modest heart,
and proving his merit by refusing it, he stands the worthier for this,
that precious modesty adorns his other ways,
and he escapes envy who fears to compare himself with others.
Seeing this, the father presses the saint more urgently,
joining to his prayers those too whose faith Martin had said
should be chosen, so that he might not even be allowed to put off
what a brotherly will, piously, with Christ inspiring it,
had urged, and the grace of a harmonious, equal authority.
So, the people having been removed, lest perhaps the crowd, if admitted,
should disturb him at prayer with confused murmuring,
or boasting display its own powers,
he took as companions only those whom the summit of office
had made his equals, and who had an equal care for prayer,
equal zeal, linked faith, united will.
The trembling father too is added, whom, longing more keenly
for Christ's gifts, his prayers had made faithful.
Then, raised up in lofty spirit but bowed in body,
setting his holy heart on high but his limbs below,
he lies low in the flesh but is strong in mind. The mind, joined
to God, climbs on high; the boasting of the flesh is crushed.
So a dissimilar path is joined in harmonious action,
so the humble hasten to where the faithful have gone before.
Without delay the saint perceived the signs of accustomed favour,
constantly rejoicing in Christ as his guest,
often opening the doors of his heart to such gifts.
Then, blessing it, he ordered oil to be brought out,
imbuing the offered juice with the nectar of words,
through which healing came into the transformed liquid.
After it had been poured into the mouth of the grateful girl,
at once the bonds of her tied tongue were loosed,
and, filling her moist throat with sudden breath,
a sweet-sounding murmur, the awaited voice, came to life.
And first he bade the father's name properly mark
her trembling speech and uncertain sounds.
This was her first word, and from the first lips of her speaking
the father snatched it and, having heard it, sank it deep into his heart.
Then with prostrate limbs he falls at [Martin's] feet
and, a suppliant, embraces his knees with outstretched arms.
And he who alone had brought prayers while the girl was silent
now returns thanks to the Lord with more than one voice.
Nor indeed is the wonder of another deed any less,
which the pouring of medicated juice
and the blessing of oil chanted over has made me remember.
This oil, whenever healing called for the help of compassion,
an equal grace sanctified for differing causes.
For as the faithful often do, with prudent heart,
a vessel filled with oil, in hope of preserving health,
they either offer to righteous men or place with devotion in holy
places, where either present working
reveals by its power the patrons who have earned the reward of martyrdom,
or where, as plain faith recalls or scripture reveals,
the Word came to the blessed cradle,
or where, cutting short the time of continuing daylight,
shuddering at the deadly crime of a dreadful people,
night poured in between and inserted sudden darkness,
or where the blessed hollows of the split rock,
rejoicing at God's touch, without the law of the tomb,
lay open, laid beneath limbs soon to rise again,
or where, rejoicing in Christ now returning from here to the stars,
the happy earth received his last footprints,
[earth] which, preserving the gifts of so sanctifying a touch,
whatever an inventive hand prepared for adornment
disdained and shook far off from its sands,
bursting the fragile lattice with dust poured through it
and dissolving the enclosures of metal stretched above:
In these places very often, where nearness allows it,
they set out peaceful liquid in clean little vessels,
to be changed by the nectar of dew poured in from above,
by which heavenly grace flows into the holy juice.
But those whom the spaces of long roads lying between
hold back, removed far off in a distant region,
believing that the Lord is not shut in by the bounds of places
and that the help of the One who pities passes all limits,
with unhesitating faith ask for the present gifts
of the present Lord, who, by the power of his favour,
does not weary the prayers of those coming to him over a long way,
but touches those who ask, everywhere brought near to him,
and does not shun the slow, [but] stands nearer to the swift,
and the mere effort of the one setting out becomes the end of the road.
Those who hold these things in their heart, in whatever part they call on him,
have the Lord's gift, whether they entrust their committed
prayers to holy men, or lay up whatever things
are to be sanctified in consecrated places. What Christ did not visit
with his holy body, he covers with his power, although he, having returned
to the heights of heaven, has long since reigned there in the body too.
Turning these things over often within herself, as faith spurred her on,
surpassing the frail sex by the strength of faith,
a woman lofty, of no womanly heart,
believed, when she offered the oil she had sent to the saint,
that the nearby compassion [of God], at the prayers of so great a minister,
would favour her prayers, with Martin praying, no otherwise
than if, carried swiftly in rapid flight,
she were bringing her prayers within the very tomb of the Lord,
embracing the banner of the cross and the wood of salvation.
Full of such faith, she carefully, into gleaming glass,
with anxious hands poured the green oil.
The descending liquid changes the snowy colour [of the glass],
and, flowing with silent gliding into the hollow below,
it rises little by little through the increase of the bright liquid,
and, its sound hushed, swells silently in its richness.
Yet so that the empty throat might stay open up to the stopper,
and the vessel not totter from being filled too full of the stream,
where the neck rises from the round body beneath,
the wide gap of the mouth still remained empty.
Then the servant took the oil and went in haste
to the saint, reporting both the prayers and the words of the petitioner.
Nor is the work of compassion delayed. Swift grace commends
the just zeal, so that no delay, even a slight one, might postpone
the faithful [woman's request] or make the favour doubtful.
And at once God showed by signs he granted
how great a gift the present blessing conferred,
lest perhaps faith should waver with trembling mind.
The men present were astonished (for Christ had bidden them be there,
chosen as witnesses for such great miracles)
that the liquid had so increased at Martin's prayer
that the wave of the swelling, rising upward,
filled the empty part with its raised flood,
and so, hastening continually to the top, yet not leaving the bottom,
it seethed as if overflowing, yet settling, stayed full,
growing with what was poured in, yet not to be emptied of what it received:
until, carrying back the happy gifts to his mistress,
the servant went exulting, and his right hand
offered the blessed man's merit, rejoicing in such great signs.
Such was the holy blessing of the illustrious prophet
when the widow, open-handed, had used up her scant supply:
it filled the empty vessels with gifts that would last,
so that, for the proofs of generous faith she had given,
she grew richer by her spending, secure in what she asked.
And indeed, though I may fear to touch the other praises
and powers of the man, at least I shall be able to tell these,
in which a similar blessing of the same juice
rightly demands the proclamations of a manifold voice.
One faith, frequent healing: it does not differ in the act,
but differs in number, equal in signs, other in gifts.
A witness is at hand, Severus, wonderful for his learned speech,
who followed Christ with the whole strength of his heart,
distinguished by the world's titles, but more famous by that
by which he scorned the world in the strength of holy faith,
powerful in nobility, but yet far more eminently
nobler by the worship of Christ than by birth of blood.
He, compressing the sacred canon and the writings
of sprawling history, enclosed in two little books everything
that had been published from the first ages, which he had run through.
He too, recounting the honours and deeds of Martin,
a careful searcher of the truth and a faithful reporter,
brought into public view the marks of so illustrious a life,
keeping the scales just with balanced weighing,
so that in speaking he would neither assert doubtful things nor keep silent about certain ones.
He very often clung to the saint, devoutly joined to him,
as the insight of the mind in the mirror of the heart is wont
to join kindred and similar forms of character.
Hence all the more must one believe that a witness is better proven
who teaches what he found out in person, since he speaks of things seen.
So, among other tokens of affection, he asked
that he might receive the special gift of holy liquid.
After the blessed man, rejoicing, had granted to his faithful friend
the help of [his] power, a memorial of his favour,
he carried it home with the reverence of faith,
believing that he was bringing home granted salvation,
and he placed it in the high part of a lofty window,
where panes stretched across shut in the clear daylight,
set against the blasts of the winds and open to the light.
Here he covered the flask with the veil of a snowy cloth,
so that the linen spread over it might stop wandering looks
that would meet the eyes, but not keep out minds.
But a servant, unaware, with the whirl of his hurrying hand,
while in haste he snatches the covering with careless effort,
dashed the glass vessel down upon the marble below.
The servant stood stunned and bloodless, his master turned pale,
and the sound comes back to the roof with a rapid beat,
and the ringing, filling everything at once with a wandering murmur,
struck against the heights, rose up from the depths.
The flask that was struck did not feel such great crashes,
and the coverings of its glassy shell remained unharmed.
So the liquid within, enclosed in its fragile garment,
hardened the outer drums of the hollow frame,
so that you would think the marble had been wholly changed into feathers
and had received that fall on soft cushions.
So, Martin, your merit, so your constant grace
devoutly receives what is sanctified, guards what is blessed.
A certain man, when the savage violence of a dreadful Molossian hound
rushed upon him, working its jaws with raging throat,
drawing back its wrinkled nostrils from the covering of its mouth,
gnashing its bared teeth with frequent growling,
frightened by such sudden terror, not with a club nor a blow
but with Martin's name alone shut its rabid mouth.
As soon as it sounded, the barking was checked and stuck fast,
the bristling hackles fell, and the eyes, threatening fiercely
and starting out, their flames suffused with blood,
laid aside their threats and closed. Then [it began] fawningly
to stroke its ears and sweep the ground with its curled tail,
and to lower its head, bowed, with neck bent.
What fierce things would not yield to your merits, Martin,
when you conquer such great rage even by your name alone?
Why now should we wonder that the hearts of savage men
yield, and human passions grow gentle toward you?
As once men were astonished that the dread power
and cruel jurisdiction of Avitianus gave way to you,
to whom savagery was all too closely bound, and whose only pleasure
was the hook, executioners, torturers, whips, chains,
the death of men, the cry of mourners and the pallor of the accused,
the devouring prison, the killing of one who confessed, the torture of one who denied.
This most savage beast with a heart all too hellish,
breathing countless slaughters from his raging breast,
roaring with merciless savagery, had entered the city
which Bishop Martin ruled with holy honour.
Bound by chains linked through their filthy necks
there clung a pale, unhappy line of grieving accused,
clashing the grating fetters against their broken limbs
and moving slow steps with bent breasts.
Leading such spectacles, this Phalaris, near to Martin,
prepares various slaughters at the judgment benches.
The raging attendants, a frenzied crowd, hurry
to seek out eagerly the instruments for savage punishments.
Some bring out vessels for hellish flames,
in which, with the dire heat of the vapour shut in,
melted pitch might feed the crackling of a fierce fire,
which, overflowing far with a flood of deadly flame,
would roast the body received in a sulphurous cave.
But others, with raging heart, were preparing the timbers
of wood stretched upward (a grim service),
so that the flesh, hanging cruelly from limbs quickly stretched,
might expose its torn joints to the torturer to be tormented,
drenching his hellish right hand with wretched blood
and spattering the grim gore through frequent wounds.
And so that the same punishment might sate a double fury,
the striker would shake the joints of the torn body,
tearing apart the bonds of the limbs, their knots broken.
But others [hurried] to bring torches, and with much grease
to smear the long bands of twisted papyrus,
not so that that light might overcome and scatter the darkness,
marking out the dark night with fire-flowing light,
but so that the funereal fire might burn the wretches,
fixing the brought-up flames on their torn limbs.
Was it fitting that these things be seen in Martin's city,
and that his peaceful mind be pierced by so great a wound,
that this report should even reach his holy ears
or that even a mere rumour should shake his devout heart?
So when his mind was struck by the funereal preparation,
and a messenger had spread these savage devices of the dread tyrant,
the forerunning signs of the fury close at hand,
a just pity ran through his whole marrow,
and the flame of compassion spread a swift heat.
And although mercy, recalling human misfortunes,
compelled him to weep for the death of the wretched accused,
there was present no less a cause of his present grief:
that the same man who was the avenger of crime
would first make himself guilty, a supporter of wickedness, by punishing guilt.
A thicker darkness had wrapped the covered world.
Welcome rest had spread gentle sleep through all the elements,
and all things drooped in dewy slumber,
and the suppressed murmurs of voices fell silent and mute.
The all-too-deep silences of midnight bristled,
and the dark gloom poured over [things] had covered their own colour,
snatching from all shapes their marks.
But Martin had no care to take rest;
instead holy prayers for human safety stood by him,
as affection spurred his mind. So he makes for the bloody
judge's frenzied threshold with urgent step.
He goes alone, fearless, through the dark silences of the vast
night and the hidden, dark ways of the bristling roads.
I believe, indeed, that all the throngs of shades gave way,
which the evil demon stirs to crimes of the night,
and that elsewhere the dreadful Molossian hounds fell gently silent,
and the barking of their terrifying mouths stuck, blocked.
So when he came to the barred threshold of the dreadful
judge, the deathly enclosure of savage fury,
lying prostrate before the house in the middle of the road, he was kept off by the closed
doors, but with his weeping he beat upon the stars.
The savage beast was breathing heavy sleep from his swollen chest,
and, with limbs stretched out in the likeness of death,
had flung his deeply torpid frame upon the bedding,
when suddenly an angelic terror shook his innards,
and a voice also burst upon the astonished ears of the stupefied man:
'Has wretched sloth weighed you down with heavy sleep,
beast, as you belch up cups of spoiled wine,
and does the load of your undigested belly swell you, sluggish,
while the servant of the Lord lies upon the dry back of the bare
earth, drenching his holy body in much dust,
look, before your doors? Do you set the bars of rest
against him, for the nightly silence of shameful sleep?'
He went rigid at the sudden vision, and quickly summoning
his attendants, ordered them to go out swiftly to the barrier,
so that they might bring back the true course of things in words of report.
But, as pleasant rest often binds and overcomes the oppressed
sense when the limbs are tied with torpor,
the slaves, going out a little way, scarcely to the first threshold,
very drowsy in their sight and tottering in their gait,
gave back deceitful mumblings in muddled words,
that no one had been found before the doors by careful search.
Again the pleasure of sleep, near and not far removed,
at once closed his drooping eyes.
Then indeed a new terror shakes his trembling heart,
and the threatening sentence of the angelic voice,
by repeating the command, forced him to rise headlong.
Nor did he choose again to risk entrusting the command.
He himself hurried with quick step to the closed threshold,
and the barred doors opened as their master unbolted them.
The venerable bishop shone out with radiant face,
displaying on his holy countenance the garlands of virtues.
Grace flourished in him, shining forth in many signs,
in religion, faith, affection, piety, modesty:
a mind cheerful in grave matters, steady and serious in glad ones,
neither stiff with harshness nor loosening its austerity in laughter,
altogether so shining always with a balanced uprightness
that anger did not make him fierce, nor kindness slack.
Such was the venerable figure that met the pale tyrant,
breaking through the clouds of the foul night.
And already, without words, his mind, conscious of so great
a crime, had betrayed what the cause of that holy labour was,
nor did it need to be laid open by entreaties. He himself first, confounded,
brought out a fearful voice from his trembling breast:
'Why, holy one, wearing out my heart this while with fear as torturer,
do you trouble it, with my sleep utterly shaken off?
You are kept far from the doors, [yet] by holy merit you burst
into the inner rooms. You stand outside in body, [yet] by right
you enter; you shake [me] with terror, you who dwell in the flesh.
Nor indeed would I deny that this is owed to my deserts,
since with hard heart I breathed out countless slaughters,
savage in your city. I pray, then, pardon one who confesses;
use your right. You wish [them] to be spared: let [it] be remitted.
Release the accused from punishment, free me from guilt.'
Without delay the loosened chains swiftly fell,
which just now had gripped the necks of the pale accused,
keeping their dying bodies for a dreadful death.
Suddenly hope, restored to the wretched for their prayer, leaps up.
With joy and fear mixed, the trembling men hesitate to believe
such great things so suddenly, but would rather believe.
Giving thanks, they vie to throw themselves at the holy knees,
to clasp his feet tenderly with suppliant arms.
He urges that thanks should rather be given to God,
and warns that Christ is the author of this deliverance,
who spares crimes in this way, if at least a true conversion
shows sorrow for the crime committed;
