for punishments remain for the guilty while the guilt endures.
With such addresses, and toiling with compassion as well,
he freed the bound from punishment, and released them from their faults.
Now truly, what tongue could worthily speak of this gift,
which the mind, too narrow for the honours of so illustrious a patron,
fears even to touch with astonished sense:
that the saint's merit so made all the hosts of the demon
tremble, and such signs of great fear were so revealed,
that whenever, going forth from the threshold of his own cell,
he had turned his steps toward the city set far off,
visiting the people entrusted to his holy governance,
or wishing to offer the mysteries of the sacred rite,
grace, going quickly ahead in swift flight,
so tormented the frightened spirits in their captive bodies,
that, though he had barely left the inner rooms of his holy dwelling,
they saw through torments, which went far ahead first,
that he would at once be present, and with the shrieking murmur of a voice
the punishment of the guilty proclaimed the judge's coming.
And when he had set his first steps in the doorway,
one could see bodies, their limbs snatched swiftly on high,
lifted up bound in airy bonds,
and the swaying weights of heavy flesh, through the void,
leave the neighbouring earth in a swift whirl,
suspended by their own punishment, yet free of any tie,
bound by the merits of prayers, hanging by their own penalties,
cry out the sins they had committed, under a silent judge.
Nor did a confession, given to a questioner's words
and extracted, betray the crimes through a trembling voice.
For the saint, bowed to the ground, passed beyond the stars in prayer,
touching the Lord in hope, but prostrate in body,
humble in heart, lofty in merit, crying out without a murmur,
a judge hidden from sight, proven by power,
at whose merit such great miracles appeared:
the guilty one hanging in the void, and the torturer in the air,
his feet stretched upward, the wool of his stiff garment
clinging tight to his covered limbs,
lest, bent into a fold or slipping backward,
it should bare the shameful parts of the hanging body.
Thus your merit, Martin, thus the holy power
and the glory of God, to be shown forth through the servants of Christ,
surpassing the earth in its honours, reigns also in the air.
It is certain too that at your supplication the clouds were dried up,
and the hanging downfall of dreadful hail stuck fast,
the flood of the thickened storm-cloud being wholly bound,
a cloud which, heavy and, by the cold of the stiff wind, its waters joined
and hardened into stones, in frequent whirlwind thus
used to hurl upon the earth rocks of solid liquid,
so that crops, shrubs, gardens, orchards, vines
were crushed by the missiles of the storms in their frequent downfalls,
and the earth, pierced through, was shaken by the mighty lash.
This plague, ranging widely through the fields of the Senones,
and accustomed every year to fulfil the law of punishment,
had stripped the battered farmland with its constant downfalls.
The pale ploughman reported his lost harvest,
lamenting the tops of the stalks broken through and through,
and the vinedresser, often groaning over a vine empty of fruit and shoot,
after the yearly hopes of his unbroken labour,
counted the losses from the clusters already swelling.
A most sorrowful mother pointed out the broken branches
where her children used to creep among the mellow little apples,
and beside the pale shoots of the parched field
the rocks rang, echoing with the lowing of the cattle.
Wasted herds roamed the empty recesses,
bearing witness to their plaintive cause with what groans they could.
Driven, then, by this evil, all the people, of every age,
desiring to secure for themselves so illustrious a patron,
humbly entreat Martin through an envoy as spokesman
that he would strive to appease God and beg pardon
for the wretched, and at last drive off the grievous plague:
enough punishment had been given; the clemency of Christ
would, at least after the scourges, take away the excessive disaster.
Nor indeed did the hope they waited for deceive the wretched.
For as soon as Martin, always joined and clinging to the Lord,
asked for the gifts of his accustomed mercy,
they felt his holy intercession: the tempest, driven off,
grew quiet, and the days shone with clear calm,
or the shoots were moistened by longed-for rains.
Nor was it confined to a short span, but over a long time,
more welcome as it commended its gifts by extended limits,
the grace lasted through four full lustra,
nor did they feel the damage of the mad storm before
the Lord, the time of the present life being closed,
took up his blessed friend to true rest.
Thus he spent in holiness the times of both lives,
before, the salvation of the earth, but now on high among the stars.
But now the far too long page of a flagging book
weakens the honours and deeds of the illustrious patron.
While, small, I speak of great things, and, sluggish, of lofty things,
I, a trembling narrator, spoil the splendour of his praise.
But what am I to do? I have vowed to run through the history in verse:
things told fear judgment; things suppressed, guilt.
Better that a reader, perhaps wearied, should leave these things aside,
than that a devout listener should look for things wholly withdrawn.
My earlier account has already touched on the cruel Avitianus:
now the order of the work is called back to him.
He, surpassing savage tyrants in dreadful ferocity,
thirsting for the grim tortures of the sorrowful accused,
spared the city of the Turones a little, being milder there.
Here only, showing traces of human feeling,
he submitted his mouth, rebellious though it was, to holy reins,
checking his inborn fury at Martin's commands.
And indeed clear proofs of this cure
appeared one day in this way. The venerable Martin
was approaching the dreadful seat under such a judge,
so that the savagery might soften and grow gentler through such
kind offices, bound by the courtesies of the holy patron.
He happened to be sitting on a very high seat,
prominent on a conspicuous throne, and swelling with exceedingly proud
ambition, when suddenly the saint, looking at him,
saw the bloody form of a bristling, foul,
mad demon, fastened to his bent-back neck,
lying prone upon it with all its weight.
When the saint touched it from afar with the breath of his blessed mouth,
and put it to flight by bringing to bear the terror of a word,
Avitianus, unaware of his companion, believed
he had received a heavy punishment in the form of a curse.
He replies: 'Do not believe that you have perhaps been branded by my
judgment, or that this is the sign of a sudden fit of temper.
This was compassion, not anger, which raged against the enemy,
[and] in pity grieves for the wretched man. This breath of ours burst
out wholly from the depths of my heart against him
whom I saw pressing this lofty bench with horrid weight
and lying prone upon your neck.
Cease now to bear the fellowship of such a robber;
trust rather in holy counsels. Let cunning, once detected,
be put to flight; let caution that has learned his tricks drive them back.
Now be ashamed to obey a guilty one, to serve one put to flight.'
With such words the door of the heart was shut against the ejected
demon, and the power of his seat was snatched away.
Then, gentler at last, a judge without a judge of his own,
and the heavy burden was shaken from his neck and thrown off.
Thus he drove out enemies, thrust from every seat,
freeing men's hearts, and not leaving temples to the fugitives either.
For whatever shrines vain error had built,
he burned to lay waste far and wide in headlong ruin.
Not a great distance away from the city mentioned before
there was a village, once the remains of an old fort,
now inhabited by servants of God and ministers of Christ.
Its former inhabitant gave it the ancient name of Ambatia.
Here the mad folly of a sacrilegious assembly had once
built a lofty temple, a work of immense labour.
Rising into a cone, a towering mass, it stretched
its wondrous work on high, so exactly finished
with stones always joined, though in close-set courses,
that the lofty weight should not sway, nor a crack open,
but a fine joinery bound the stones laid against one another.
All the more did those lacking reason marvel with astonished minds
at the craftsman's skill. Thus a foolish, shameful
religion grew strong, worshipping as divinity only
the talent and genius of a god named after the builder.
This temple, then, the holy Martin had ordered
to be pulled down. He reproaches the faithful priest
for orders long neglected. Yet he modestly says
that these commands could not be carried out. He shows that these things
are hard enough for worn-out monks and a few ministers of God,
things that crowds gathered with difficulty from an emptied countryside
or toiling cohorts could scarcely accomplish.
In these words a just excuse was fully plain.
Yet hope was not broken. He does not make vows
to summon peoples, nor hasten to lead troops
gathered from the whole world to the village of Ambatia.
He calls on heavenly help. All hope is in him
who rules heaven and earth, whom the air serves as a soldier,
and to whom the elements keep an abiding fear.
Once again, then, the bristly garments, wont to pierce
the reclining skin with goads, fleeces woven of stubborn
harshness with stiff threads to make wounds,
again sleepless groans, again fasts
renewed with food put off, and joining the night's labour
again to the sun soon to follow.
No long delay put off this prayer. Look! When day returned,
a violent storm roars around the temple,
the clouds bursting into rivers with a whirlwind of winds.
The clouds are split apart as lightning is flung out,
and a mass of waters gathered above the heights
crashes against the [building's] frame with a hoarse-sounding whirl,
and the battle of the storm-clouds gives forth a sharp crash.
The earth trembled and, shaken from the lowest depth,
spat out the hanging foundations of the mass set upon it,
scattering the ruin far and wide from its joints
and rolling the fragments of the shattered mass down the slope.
O you, greatly beloved of God! At your plea Christ
once dried up the clouds as they bent low in the lofty air.
At your prayers again swift storms returned,
and black clouds girded with heavy winds,
bidden to spare the crops, bursting mighty structures,
soft to the grasses and merciless to hard stones.
Nor will this merit be less, nor, with a cause not unequal,
the glory unlike, imitating equal triumphs.
The very lofty supports of a column raised
an idol's image far into the heights with joined stones,
so that the figure, higher and more exalted on that throne,
might look down on the wretched people with a feigned divinity.
This mass too Martin desired to overthrow,
but all equipment had been lacking for such a wish;
yet his hope remained ever swift [to turn] to the Lord.
So, as with nimble mind he flew back to the heavens
and asked swift help from the king of the heavens,
a fiery column, like in appearance but unlike in light,
fell down and smashed the fragile ruin,
a sulphurous flame rolling up crackling ashes,
raising a smoking cloud from the burnt dust
and a steam overflowing as the mass was consumed.
So, Martin, with the glowing sky, so with the whirlwind,
you link twin triumphs, by cloud or by fire.
Nor is it a wonder that the Lord should fulfil his promises to a faithful servant,
to so holy a servant, he who had once said
to his servants, greatly astonished at such miracles,
that he would give these proofs of true faith:
that those who believed would show signs greater than these.
What wonder is it that the favouring Lord accomplished the same things
through his servants, he who, deigning to promise more to his devout ministers,
called lofty hearts upward?
For as the page of the heavenly book relates,
bearing witness to a woman's faith, after many floods
of blood and a sad wasting, her body consumed,
swift health returned at the touch of a garment:
so the glory of the same deed was given to Martin,
but with God healing, who now too, high in the citadel
of his starry throne, is shown to be touched through the members
which cleave to the eternal head in holy union.
What was not gentle to the devout man, what monsters were not subject
to the faithful man? Serpents often obeyed when commanded,
and no inborn fierceness lay beneath their conquered venom.
A dreadful snake was swimming across the nearby shallows
and furrowing the glassy waters. Its head stood out from the waves
with its neck. With its breast it split the surface
of the river in haste. The rest of its length through the blue
bent its slippery coils with varied motion,
twisting the curved spirals of its smooth tail
and darting its flickering tongue, intent on wounds.
When Martin saw it, scarcely in the middle of the water,
hurrying ever nearer to approach the adjoining land,
he forced it with these words to go swiftly back again,
bound by the power of God and the name of Christ:
'I command you by no means to make further
for the forbidden bank.' The evil beast stood still in the middle of the current,
and a stiff numbness bound its broken limbs,
and its members slowly stuck fast in captive swimming,
until, the surge of the obstructing flood shut off,
its languid neck floated on the deep that was let go,
and the sluggish channel bore the half-dead snake back.
And would that with like power my own venom,
which the slipperiness of a badly spent life has corrupted,
always plunging my sins into the rushing world,
the faithful compassion of the holy patron might turn back,
and force it again to remember the salvation it forgot,
lest my limbs sink headlong into the muddy deep
and my stained body be soaked in the flood of vices,
but that my steps, steady on high at the bank of virtues,
may stand firm in faith, and trample earthly joys,
and long to escape with swift effort the things that flow away.
With this prayer alone I shall linger a little by the rivers,
while recalling them I run through the titles of my famous patron,
at whose merit the flood of waters, as ordered,
rejoicing to submit itself, obeyed his holy commands.
His fasts, kept up continually through the year,
the solemnities of holy Easter relaxed a little.
On these days only did he afflict his limbs more gently.
Then alone he took a small fish as food.
But while the occasion was being kept for signs to come,
the customary catch of the service failed his wish.
When he learned that the fishermen's labour had passed in vain
and the nets stretched out had floated through an empty deep,
from the complaining words in the murmur of the mourners
(for the deacon present was, with faithful mouth, a sufficient
supporter of the rest, whom the more urgent care of this
service had made, wakeful through the time of the past night
and weary as part of the present day was spent,
present as witness of the common labour):
as his anxiety moved the saint's tender heart,
stirred by holy grief he said, 'Go and, skilfully,
search the river, quickly crossing its streams.
Now the nets will enclose a captive prey for you.'
Without delay, trusting the word of so great a master,
the deacon hurries. Hope was restored to his anxious wish,
nor did the catch, though delayed, fail the hurrying man.
For as soon as he enclosed the nearby shallows with a small net,
the line, struck, trembled as the cork floats moved,
betraying a prey entangled above the trackless blue.
Quickly he drew to the near shore the enmeshed
pike, rejoicing. Then, bending forward with his whole breast,
he puts his wet arms around the slipping fish.
The slippery prey barely holds in his bared arms,
and, thrashing, almost slips out of his wet grasp,
until, little by little leaving its native element,
dying, it breathed out its thin life into the air,
and, quivering, opened its mouth in a feeble gape,
flapping with the sluggish motion of its tail flung back.
The joy of the monks was astonished at their wish [fulfilled],
who had come out from the neighbouring cells to so great a spectacle,
and, in good will, had believed that the word spoken from the holy breast
would be fulfilled with such a guarantor.
O truly mirror of eternal virtue! From him
these gifts flow to you, who once bade the disciples,
weary from labouring in vain by night, to draw
the nets, sending a numerous prey into the nets,
enclosing fish chosen for the holy banquet,
whom, snatched utterly from the whirl of the middle of the world,
the teaching of the holy faith would draw to the Lord.
Often God wished illustrious men to make known the lofty merit
of the blessed man, so that with them as witnesses,
men whom the glory of the world had raised high,
the signs of his powers, made known to the peoples, might shine the more clearly.
For Arborius, then famous for the summit of the prefecture he had held,
saw, while [Martin] was offering the holy rites to God,
Martin's hand gleam red, flashing with the light of shining
gems, and a flashing light
clothe the fiery right hand with precious purple,
and the clash of stones striking together crackle.
Not such gems have adorned the standards of generals,
nor do such diadems encircle the brows of kings,
but such as the Lord's sentence, at the end, sets
as well-earned gems in the bright crowns of the saints.
Nor is there doubt that by the uprightness of his outstanding faith
he shines beyond what is human with a varied flower of virtues,
whom the blessed page of the historical book attests
deserved the comfort of an angel's word face to face.
For when, deeply grieving, he was returning from the city of Trier,
in which, while he dreaded the death of wretched men
at the hands of an angry king, whose lives he was begging from [the king] himself,
he, compelled to relax his own strictness a little,
had looked more gently on the Ithacian fault,
driven to spare mercifully a condemned cause
and to restore again new bonds of holy peace:
him, then, so greatly afflicted with grief, revisiting him,
an angel, manifest face to face in speech and countenance,
kindly brought comfort to his sorrowing friend,
soothing his anxious heart with the words he offered,
teaching by counsel what was to be changed, absolving what had been done.
Thus, marking the heralding of the foremost prophet,
the heavenly messenger with holy mouth
made Zechariah learn beforehand of the rising of his holy son,
promising that his voice would come back after the silence imposed on him.
In the end a like order revealed no unlike merit,
and as offspring fell to the one, so grace fell to the other,
shining more brightly with the added light of miracles.
For often the spirits driven from a captive breast,
not yet compelled by the words or voice of one present,
were terrified by the blessed nearness of the holy cell
and by the power that went far beyond that blessed dwelling.
So, spread out very widely, the signs shone far and wide,
bearing witness to the Lord's present favour,
not content with the land alone, but quite often
breaking far out upon the very waves with Martin's glories.
Sailors tossed in a vast whirlwind saw,
while the more violent wave of the mad storm raged,
how much the saint could help even by his name alone.
A ship was ploughing the middle of the sea on the Tyrrhenian expanse,
hastening with sails spread over the blue.
The driven prow was cleaving the deep beneath it,
bursting the whitening waves with its opposing breast,
leaving long tracks of foaming paths,
when suddenly clouds spread out and covered the sky,
damp fleeces wove a blackening lattice,
and the light, hidden deep in a pitch-black cloud, perished.
Mighty winds set to overturning the sea,
and soaked sands are mixed with the red waves.
Lofty masses [of water] are shattered by the violent whirlwind.
Rolling heaps hung high on the lifted wave,
raising unstable hills far too high,
as they fall back, are broken and dissolve in repeated collapses,
and, crashing down, give back countless roars far off.
The sails fall; the rigging resounds with a quivering shriek.
Now [the ship] lies hidden as the mountain [of water] is cut off near the clouds,
now again it totters, perilously hanging on a high ridge,
fearing a doubtful fall into either deep;
but other waves strike the resisting sides,
and, broken against the battered lattice of planks, rebound,
filling the torn ship with such constant spray.
The violence of the sea wrenches off and shakes loose the rudder,
flinging the helmsman far away. Dread shakes the hearts
of the terrified, tearing their insides with trembling motion,
and wetting their pale cheeks not with spray alone.
Confused groans, and murmurs of tearful voices,
and the sighs of weepers broken by constant sobbing
lament with one like complaint as death draws near.
Meanwhile a certain man, driven by extreme terror,
but not yet instructed in the reason of the true faith,
asked for heavenly help with this cry:
'God unknown to me, but known by the merit of the holy
servant whom I revere, through whom your glory shines,
God of Martin, have mercy, drive off the danger,
rescue us. For the holy bishop, as I remember, proved
by frequent miracles that all things come easily to you.'
Without delay the seas fell, the waves laid flat,
and a level plain of calm waters lay still,
and the west wind, gently driving the torn ship with a moderate breeze,
set it in the anchorage it longed for.
So Christ proved the merit of his servant through all the elements
and spread abroad the glories of his holy friend,
glorifying his famous name over the pathless blue.
Nor is it any wonder that Martin's faith, with God's favour,
could be proved by so many things, if ever,
wakeful in blessed vigils, with all the power of prayer,
he had in person brought happy petitions to the Lord,
if grace was able to shine out through his name alone
for one wholly ignorant and far removed.
Although the page, striving toward the highest praise,
may draw back its foot in amazement and fear
to climb with poor words to so great a mass of miracles,
by which the saint is shown to have healed not one man, but at once a whole
household by his healing intercession:
the witness is at hand, Lycontius, lofty in the office of a famous prefecture,
ascribing these gifts [to Martin] with grateful lips,
whose household a single plague, ranging widely
with manifold ruin, had overwhelmed. Everywhere the wasting
bodies of the half-dead, cast out in every part,
crowded the dreadful thresholds with their weary limbs.
Grim pain everywhere, and frequent sighs, constant
weeping, and groans wrung from the very depths
of the cavern of the breast, breath that racked the flanks,
and continual vomiting, parched skin, a flame lodged in the marrow
setting the stomach on fire, a heavy wave of fever-heat.
Those sad bodies of the half-dead grew pale
beside a neighbouring corpse, and the crowd of the dying,
sadder for such an example, dreaded the deaths of their kin.
But others, wretched, feared even to touch their dear ones
when lifeless, in an all too trembling duty,
lest the spreading contagion sow grievous diseases.
Fear had withdrawn these from service, but grief had
hemmed in the anxious hearts of those with manifold mourning.
And those who had laid the limbs in their last tombs,
put off for no long time to a like death,
carried like diseases to the sorrowful thresholds.
Physicians' hands availed nothing, nothing the herbs that by their juices
had often worked great cures for the sick.
So the master, confounded by such destruction of his people
and distrusting his own prayers, strives to appease
the Lord by the intercession of the saint and the merit of his patron,
pleading the lamentable disaster with Martin as his advocate.
He, though he felt all too keenly the burden of a hard case,
the judge being already offended, yet in his mercy
received with anxious care the petitioner's troubled prayers.
Nor did he cease, tormented by unbroken toil,
to wear down his dry limbs, the marrow drained,
and to beat the hard ground with prostrate effort,
doubling his accustomed fasts with added penances,
not closing his eyes even in light sleep,
goading his wasted flesh with bristly haircloth,
until the Lord, moved by the zeal of so great a friend,
at last wholly ended his anger and grew mild,
giving back the happy gifts of longed-for health,
and the crowd of his household, embracing their rejoicing master,
welcomed him, testifying their joy with all their prayers,
as he told the glories and deeds of his famous patron.
He, after the ruin had been driven off by Martin's prayer,
hastening thus to repay gifts to the deserving saint,
brought a hundred pounds of silver to the threshold of the aforesaid [saint],
repaying the reward with the gifts he offered,
so that even a small fee might prove the physician's merit,
and the wishes of the generous and grateful man be shown in his zeal.
The saint, rejoicing in the kindness of his dear friend,
did not refuse these rewards that testified to the love of a devoted heart,
since he prudently considered the giver's loss,
that the gifts sent ahead might bring back the fruit of faith;
nor yet did he take them for his own use,
lest the wish to possess should stain the saint's mind,
but entrusting them to God he stored them up in high heaven,
so that now, freeing captives from hard punishments,
shut out from his holy threshold, given to the redeemed,
the money, being counted, kept faith, being spurned, kept strictness.
Go on, then, following what you sent ahead, claiming what was promised,
bishop, on high to the bright citadel of heaven,
you who have won a starry home and a glowing crown,
you who were able to bind all the rage and the whole fury
of the dread demon into a little fly.
But we shall always venerate the limbs present with us,
until you return with your body to eternal life,
joined to the tombs of the saints, destined to be joined to their crowns.
You have scarcely been able to hide only your face from us,
remaining with us in loving care. Peoples in throngs
often visit you; healing lives before your face;
the gifts of longed-for health are at hand at once.
Words are silent, but signs shine. If in body you are
withdrawn a little from sight, in power you are seen present.
I pray that you will always be present, manifestly, in the heart
of your wretched poet, so that when meditation has finished
the song, the written discourse may hold your praise.
BOOK SIX.
You renew my care for murmurs to be renewed,
while you prove your life by miracles, a bishop not enclosed
by the law of death, and surviving your flesh without flesh,
you are seen, sought, touched and held.
While you bestow present help, you show your honour,
standing by the one who seeks, and never hidden from the one who prays.
How well the spirit, close at hand, embraces the limbs nearby,
and grace floods the holy stone!
Nothing is far when faith knocks. Crying hearts
plead their own cases without voice or murmur.
He reads the words of the mind who looks into the thought and visits
the heart and surveys the secret cavern of the breast.
Recalling them earlier, I recorded his deeds in five little books,
gathering at least a few out of many. What fraction
of such great glories has come to our knowledge? What has one man attained?
With how great a reward he repays slight labour!
Again I attempt his praises with unworthy mind:
so great are the wishes my bosom bears, through the goodness of the patron.
Loving grace goes before merit: the palm is held,
and the burden is not felt. Not yet has the care of the labour
been tasted by me: that he bids me be willing is already a pledge of the gift.
O how many tongues of greater eloquence could
have adorned this work with good! He does not allow his accustomed
songs to be rejected: he believes good the things he knows to be his.
For it is certain that he himself ordered what his interpreter, sent by him,
thinks should be attempted, his companion, clinging [to him],
and ever revering the precepts of so great a master,
a happy teacher who will live in everlasting age.
He does not tell the uncertainty of report, nor does he credulously hasten
to spread the breezes of rumour through attentive ears.
He proves things seen before his eyes, he stands as a most faithful witness,
as champion of the faith he reports miracles he observed,
offered to his own eyes and granted to his prayers.
Hither, from different parts of the world, eagerly
throngs gather; thousands multiply numerous causes
and repeat their prayers. Swift grace gives
the help of the loving-kindness they longed for. They rejoice exultantly
that, having travelled the way, they carry off swift fruit of their labour.
Now truly, minds possessed by a raging demon
are summoned hither by help, swift healing snatches them hither.
The guilty are set before [the judge] and tremble. Confession cries out,
wrung out by command. Under the judge a wholesome punishment
is seen, and the invader is ordered to utter his own words
in another's body from the captive mouth.
The judge is felt but not seen, the impious enemy [is felt].
An exile, he hastens to depart from the prey snatched from him,
and fleeing, to vanish amid the pressing punishments.
Bonds of air bind the entangled body.
Limbs you thought loose you will marvel to see bound.
Things seen will confirm faith. The one whom punishment has bound
shows his torments, constricted with his arms entwined,
and the obstacles set against his fastened limbs strike him.
What of when the railings, sinking along the track of their steps,
support an airy course? Swaying bodies run,
and the hollow air carries up the flight laid upon it.
Indeed, into the well too, which, enclosed in the church itself,
hollow, belches forth health-giving waters from its spring,
bodies are thrown, driven in a headlong leap,
the guilty one forcing them downward, who, pressing down the crown,
thrusts the head, going before its limbs, into the depth
of the pool, and bears hard on the brain with the weight of the limbs.
But who would not see, when the submerged bodies rise again,
that an outstretched embrace had opened, and that the props of favour
had unlocked their arms, softly receiving the falls?
The plunderer weighs down the limbs; mercy preserves the life.
The zeal of help is more evident than the robber's punishment.
Whoever you are who totter with wavering faith, take note: the bodies
rise again and are drawn back to life by Martin's prayer.
The depth only swallows the limbs of the wretched,
and the well with its gaping mouth does not crush those shut in it.
But why do I speak of wells? The native river bears witness to
a work of wonderful power, the river which, joined to the walls of the city,
laps the stones with its neighbouring streams.
Flowing between, it divides the cell and the tomb,
and sets a wide expanse between the separated places,
navigable, and, spreading itself with vast flood into the likeness of a strait,
and setting its banks far apart from each other,
it wearies the eyes with the farther view,
and tires arms, however strong, in swimming across.
To this river, from the church which holds the holy limbs
and keeps the blessed body for eternal praise,
a raging demon made its way with a wretched body,
meaning to drown the seized prey in the nearby flood.
But such great compassion allows the bloody one nothing
and takes from the dire tyrant his most savage rights.
A hardened path is trodden; the water, made solid, resists
the steps, and the wave does not wash the hurrying feet.
Across the river the crowds marvelled at the dry clothes,
and the cell joyfully received the man to be cleansed,
the cell which long ago was the happy host of an angelic life.
Nor did the disturbed minds retain anything done at that time
once they returned to themselves and recovered their senses.
Often it produces the sounds of the Huns, and the mutterings
of threatening men, and words cut short in savage abbreviation.
He gained help openly before a witness without knowing it,
unaware of the gift, and saved by so great a gift.
Often tongues bent to foreign mutterings
were seized by the spirit, possessor of the wretched mouth,
so that the words of Gauls flowed in Greek speech,
and in speaking they expressed a people not known even by name.
Would anyone think that this man spoke of his own mind,
who utters things unknown to him? From the cave of the breast
the possessing power bellows and bends the subdued tongue,
as strings sound out the movement that the plectrum runs over,
and the threads of the strings speak at the command of the hand.
O how often, under God's pressure, they confess what is to come,
and those whose deceit lies always delight
are forced to speak a truth wrung from them by the Lord!
What a punishment it is to speak plainly! The command draws out
the voice, and the oppressed will yields to the order.
A man illustrious in valour, but in kindly character
more famous, and great in faith, by which he stands the higher,
Aegidius, a hostile siege had hemmed in with a large host,
a siege that had fenced the walls with arms set against them,
shutting out help and pressing the besieged with force,
so that division would give less strength to the besieged
and allied camps could not join together for war.
But by the Lord's protection, cast down, there are routed
thousands, and the host that went out from the double gates
restores its solid strength, with the leader safe.
Meanwhile the sad neighbourhood, with trembling fear,
grew pale at the peril of so great a noble, and all
the anxious concern of fearful peoples hung in suspense,
while each thought he would endure a like storm,
and whatever rests on one man wavers in that one.
So someone, as it happened, from among those whom a fouler rage
had drawn to the wish of drinking blood in slaughter,
seized, as if by a headlong whirlwind, at the Lord's nod,
and outrunning the swift winds beyond blasts and clouds,
set out the sequence of events from the captive body,
proclaiming that at the same moments, at the same time,
the city had been freed from siege by Martin's prayer,
and that God had granted him both people and leader.
Soon the truth became plain and proved the sequence.
It was the very day, the same hour, nothing out of order,
and punishment compelled the unwilling enemy not to deceive.
As Balaam, wishing to curse the Lord's people,
blessed the rejoicing assembly when God wrung it from him,
in no other way, and in the very same order of events, came
a messenger, [saying] that that city was freed from so great a siege,
the city which subdued the headlong Rhône with a pliant bridge
and joined both banks with a connected track,
to give a dry path, which presses on boats
from above, and the swaying way hangs over the pressed-down river.
This city too, holy one, joined to the patron who was present,
you rescue, and you force the frightened one to confess your prayers,
which it would not wish granted to you. The guilty one stands by, and, swifter
than the East wind, having lost the prospect of the slaughter he longed for,
is not silent, and becomes the herald of a deliverance hateful to himself.
This too the reckoning revealed when the hours were examined:
it was accomplished and announced, as events showed, at the very moment.
Now indeed, how great is the healing that brings cures to all,
not brought by a healing hand, nor by wholesome juice,
enduring neither the edge of iron, nor a draught of herbs,
nor the fire of melted sulphur snatched to the sore,
but flowing with the word as healer, and rightly proven
by faith of swift power, which, standing close by,
invites the fearful by all [its works], while it heals those who obtain [it].
Here the blind marvelled at the gifts of light unknown,
here the lame at swift running with a body made vigorous,
here the deaf at the new distinctions of the voice bestowed:
as many causes as had brought ruin, so many gifts restore
health. Always help stands by more abundantly
than the sufferings, and present protection drives off danger.
A paralysed girl experienced such great healing,
who had afflicted her wretched parents with long grief.
For the violence of the disease had taken away all use
of her limbs, and, deadening all her sinews at once beforehand,
had cast her lifeless limbs utterly upon the bed,
and living only by a groan, with weary breath
and tiny gasps she shook her panting chest.
She, brought to the saint's merit by her parents' hands,
lay, pitiable, near the neighbouring tomb.
Now they wet their faces, dripping with alternate weeping,
and vie in turn in a poured-out river of tears.
Mercy moved the saint. Scarcely had the light touch
of blessed oil reached the wretched limbs,
when the feet sprang up, the sinews gained strength,
and the arms, made strong, felt the longed-for movements,
and the raised hands played with loosened fingers.
At once the wretched [parents] seize the joys they had prayed for,
and, so trembling, scarcely believe what they would rather believe.
Her face changes again with a better serenity,
and the new marvels of her clear countenance draw [all eyes].
Yet decency did not long keep this merit.
Those who now were burdening the threshold with constant vows,
promising a quick return after such great rewards,
and that the cost of the poor would soon be lightened by their gifts,
the poor whom the holy bishop generously feeds and clothes,
while in devotion he provides the customary aid to the needy
and his ready will grows rich by its expenses,
when they snatched up the dire poison of the ancient snake,
and the same serpent who once persuaded Eve
compelled these too, with the spite of a like counsel,
to trample on neglected faith, then their depraved will,
given over to evil counsels, to the words of men who wanted otherwise
unhappily yielded, to foul lies,
unmindful of the favour witnessed and wholly forgetting it.
It sought idol rites with a mad heart,
changed the planned journey, and the vigorous girl
it snatched from the author of life, and to the dire robber
handed her over, ungrateful to faith but subject to the enemy.
But when the deadly tombs of the tyrant of Tartarus
were seen from afar by the deceived girl in her error,
she fell, and, stripped of the gift of so great a patron,
was given over to her own diseases, her body crushed,
until the girl, healed by the earlier gift,
was seized by death, doubled by evils and owed to punishment.
How much better, if, recalling the gifts of such great healing,
even her present life had called her to eternal life,
so that, believing, she had rightly remembered the gospel word,
by which the servant healed by the Lord's gift was ordered
to avoid his sin, lest he go back into it again
and atone for the fault with heavier punishment.
Sometimes he compelled the unjust by just terror
to feel the power of God. For often the rebellious,
if precepts do not yet rule them, are at least compelled by blows.
When suddenly Gaul, terrified by fear of a greater danger,
had to endure the Huns as auxiliaries
(for you could hardly bear an ally who is harsher than an enemy
and drives off the treaty joined with him by his savagery),
one of them, driven by the goads of a raging demon,
burst, a wicked robber, into the Lord's holy church.
Then, daring to profane God's altar with unholy step,
and following the frenzied desires of his gaze,
he tore away with plucking right hand the holy crown,
which, joined close by, showed the saint's merit,
representing that crown which he received with Christ as judge,
shining on high in the starry citadel of heaven.
But the eyes felt the guilt, because, messengers to the heart,
those lights had wished to hide away the spoil they had looked upon.
He sinned by his gaze in triumph, and could not see
what he had seized, and the pleasure, withdrawn, left his eyes.
He groaned that his sight was besieged as if by night in daytime,
and, seeking the comfort of the surrounding light,
grieved that the nearby sun was thickening into darkness.
Why is he amazed that his sight is shut in sudden gloom?
He was blind already, when he saw wrongly what he would seize.
But when he revealed the crime to a friend who asked,
and laid bare his deeds to a questioning companion,
following a guide going ahead, as the night compelled,
he sought the blessed altar with a different intention,
now tamed by his own disaster and nearer to salvation.
Having confessed his misdeeds, the guilty man, wishing himself
to condemn himself by a wholesome judgment, seems to have earned
pardon from this, that he confesses he has earned punishment.
Grief makes amends for what deserved punishment: he restores what he seized,
so that he may get back what he lost; he receives his own, and offers what he took.
The perverted mind had punishment, the converted one healing.
But another, thirsting for slaughter, more violent in his anger,
more fevered than the demon which, shut up in a captured body,
in its fury was oppressing a wretched man by the law of Tartarus,
struck the body possessed by the deadly demon,
an enemy all the more cruel than so dread a lodger,
and plunged his bloody sword into the pierced breast.
But the same madness and fury, persisting,
turned the foaming sword and the right hand dripping with blood
against the author of the crime, the slaughter scarcely done,
and with the blade laid open the hiding-places of so great a crime,
and searched through his entrails for the deed so wickedly conceived.
How swiftly a speedy vengeance proved the judgement,
and how quickly retribution joined itself to such an offence!
Let no one think these things harsh, since a few
signs sharpen fear, punishment terrifies, and dread is a healing.
Rejoicing to add adornment to the holy altars,
the people were hastening, vying in their exultant zeal.
But when so great an effort
was attempting to move some beautiful columns to the threshold of the holy church,
a certain man, rebelling with blinded heart against such eager work,
made ready to go against it, and dared to delay such undertakings,
driven by the prompting of a raging demon,
threatening his wife besides, that he would make her pay with her tears
for the finished work, since she, as it happened, living on a neighbouring
estate, had given tools that were sought for the work.
Without delay, into the clear shallows of a little stream
he was thrown from his headlong horse, and found no waters
that could submerge his prostrate body.
Doomed to drown, he sought out waters, and on the thin current
he lay face down: dying, he swallowed the sands that he had pressed.
A shipwreck without a ship snatched him, a whirlpool without a river.
The elements recognise God. Nothing could then
be falsely ascribed to chance, which the command alone had accomplished.
Surely it was not the threats sent before that moved those tears
of hers as she wept for your death, but she laments as, earlier,
a prophet of a hateful omen, you foretold what was to come.
You go before our columns, no longer hindering them,
nor do you snatch away the church's adornment, you who were to be snatched off to the tomb.
But the people, devoted with greater faith and pressing on,
hastened the outstanding work. With the power proved,
the judgement shone forth, and present devotion grew.
Now, with terror laid aside, you will read, you who are corrected by perils,
and you will count up the gentle gifts of our outstanding patron,
and after the poison struck down with the serpent vanquished
you will first rejoice in the juice of nectar-sweet oil.
Whenever the close neighbourhood of the holy tomb
received it near at hand, true grace changed the liquid
and brought swift healings in haste.
The blessed bishop had brought and offered oil
with unhesitating faith, that that Spirit might moisten it
and steep it with the new breath of nearby favour:
Perpetuus, a worshipper of the Lord not only in name,
and following the examples set before him by his holy master.
When, with reverence, he wished to bring this aid to men's health
and apply this proven good to all remedies,
dust quickly scraped from the blessed marble
and mixed in doubled the strength of the holy oil,
so that thus the power, twinned in the sprinkled liquid,
might, by contact, increase faith, and, joined to it, health.
But when the neighbourhood felt even a tiny crumb,
swift grace raised up the oil it touched,
and the swelling, overflowing, boiled up. Abundant
plenty increased what had grown when the gift was brought before [the tomb].
Rising higher than its mouth, the outpouring wet the enclosure.
And yet grace, overflowing, did no harm,
both flowing over what lay beneath and ever full for those it filled.
This glory never stains the clothes it soaks:
they keep a greater brightness, like Siloam beheld,
and bear witness to so great a work. Let no one wash out
what power has marked, written down with so great a proof.
Nor is this praise confined to the place: grace, following the faithful,
sent its lofty titles even into the air.
Even the storms felt the saint's merit,
and the terror of hail stuck fast in the thickened clouds,
and a gentler anger spared the places it was to lay waste.
A certain man, confident that he would bring away true safety
if he were allowed to carry anything from the threshold of the holy church
to his own house, received, a rejoicing servant,
the blessed, health-giving reward of wax.
His glad faith learned by experience what it had felt
with the whole heart: the awaited hope brought back help.
His protected field escaped those stony darts
of liquid and the icy lashes of congealed water,
covering the crops by this sowing, which, buried in the earth,
stretched out spreading branches as a votive covering.
All the neighbourhood was astonished at the favour granted,
and the power, already known, was revealed by true signs.
Not with a hundred tongues could I
tell all these praises, or unfold such great palms of mighty deeds.
Nor must I knock at the oracles of lying Phoebus,
nor wait for the lyres of the made-up sisters.
Let another fill us for the proclaiming of such great praise:
let the Spirit give both words and joys to our heart.
That I may be able to sing what is true, let my patron, my Muse,
cherish me, and let his grace quicken my understanding,
so that I may not be overcome by the splendour of the work, nor,
overwhelmed by so great a light, turn my unsteady eyes from the light,
but may sing lofty and heavenly things with clear understanding.
Believe the holy God, reader, in what you hesitate
to believe from us, and you will know that all these things are easy for Christ,
who gave them and commanded them to increase the saint's titles.
The people had grown accustomed to pay a solemn homage
to the holy man every year, when the circle of the returning year
exultantly renewed the mysteries of holy Easter.
Great veneration of the cell invites them to hasten,
the cell which lay open as a faithful hostess to so outstanding a saint,
possessed by that angelic man. Bowed faces grow wet
with weeping, and with tears they seek the saint's footprints.
What places he touched while singing psalms, what places he pressed while praying,
they wish to recall from here; where he took his food,
relaxing his immense fasts with a scanty taste;
which cell, with heavenly aid, gave rest after his vigils
and, granting brief sleep to his limbs,
refreshed his lofty mind with a wakeful vision.
Hither the shepherd rejoices, exultant, to lead his people.
The throng, taken on board many boats, crosses the water,
and the waves are hidden beneath the fleet. Hither every sex and age
is present. The houses stand empty of keepers.
From all the dwellings a mutual faith stands by.
Meanwhile the author of death and of sin, steeped
in the spite of his envy, makes ready to go against
these efforts, and attacking a laden ship,
sank it in mid-stream and in the vast whirlpool,
engulfing everything at once, snatched into the deep,
and dragging the entangled throng along the river's course.
How exultantly he awaited that disaster, and with what triumph
he counted the longed-for deaths of a countless slaughter,
snatching little ones torn from the breasts of their nurses,
and scattering wandering ruin over the pathless blue,
seeing others, their necks weighed down by the grip,
sink the body their arms had clasped, drowned,
and these dragged along by their now soaked clothes, yet seeking heaven
with their eyes, and driving off the inrushing waters with a murmur.
Meanwhile a united cry in the name of Martin
calls down heavenly help. All the crowd
falls prostrate and floods the damp sands with weeping.
So joyful a day owed special joys
to the sorrowing, and an exceptional gift at a solemn time.
At once, in the midst of the waves, a gentler Spirit was present
and snatched away from dread death its wicked rights.
The liquid held up the drifting limbs. Made firm for their saving,
the water bore up their bodies on its waves. Not struck by swimming,
nor furrowed and wounded by alternating hands,
it carried its motionless burden and brought joys back
to the banks, and gladly counted the safety it had conveyed.
The mother recognised her son, the infant clung
to its mother, and the father cherished his children in his embrace.
Brother, mother, master, servant, lady, kinsman
came together with converging steps, and a voice resounding
sang thanks and praised God in holy hymns.
Hardly does anyone dare at once to believe what is seen,
and with trembling wish consults his doubting eyes.
Nor was faith broken by terror: they hasten to the river.
Quickly a new grace restores vigorous strength.
They do not wish to change their dress. In the same clothes
they rejoice, and faith is not chilled by a soaking garment.
So the farther bank, gladdened by so great a triumph,
joyful and believing, said, 'Let us sing to the Lord.'
The unharmed prey sings; the drowned predator remained [below].
Behold, once more the Lord, the Jordan split by a chasm,
opened a divided path, and commanded the people, through the river,
to join themselves close to the ark that went before.
Returning to its source, the flood turned back its streams
and, halting its course, hastened flowing back toward its rising.
The people trod these places, the sands trampled,
which the anxious sailor had run with oar and sail.
What ways of land and sea has the glory of this name
not penetrated, roused with swift leap,
having gone beyond the ways of the ocean and the ridges of the vast sea
passable to sailors? Snatched away by mighty storms,
a ship, carried far into an unknown deep,
beyond the ways of men and fleets, had rushed headlong,
by the thrust of a whirlwind, onto a sea bound fast in torpor.
No hope gave a way out. For with the glue of its liquid
the sea, motionless and resisting, held the timbers
in a siege of the sea. Longing for winds, the sailors
would have preferred the aid of a tempest and the rage of a whirlwind,
making vows for a storm in the midst of the waves.
But no power of escape is given to the wretches.
So sluggish a shipwreck holds them, without any motion.
The ship that floats on the sea does not float free. Fixed in the waves
is a hateful stillness. What the sea holds up, it blocks,
neither carrying the ship on with a thrust nor swallowing it in a chasm.
No hope of escape appears. For in the waves
a torpid guard keeps the prey bound fast by the waters.
The one hope is God alone. Whatever he created,
he also rules. The elements keep the command of their creator.
At the Lord's nod things stirred up suddenly grow still,
and torpid things swiftly learn unaccustomed motions,
and his command gives law to things set in order before.
A certain man, following report with better sense,
had learned of Martin's titles, as fame spread them through the world,
and of miracles full of holy deeds.
He, under the pressure of misfortune, thinking the only safety
was to cry to the true God, prayed thus, as it happened,
raising to heaven his eyes, wet with a fountain of tears,
he lifts [them], and, joining the inmost depths of his heart to his eyes,
says: 'Look upon the wretched, one true hope of salvation.
O God, have mercy for Martin's sake, you who through him have scattered
so many signs of divine favour among the peoples,
and, proving his merit by miracles, have commanded
his renown to pass beyond the lands, famous even across the seas.
May he loosen or relax the bonds of the ship
by his intercession, may he make the parted waters give way,
and the flowing sea at last grow thin in its deep.'
Without delay a mighty force of wind swiftly gliding in
drove out the ship, snatched away, through the cleft deep,
and carried it with an easy breeze over the pathless blue,
and soon in the longed-for anchorage of a harbour refreshed
those carried out and carried back alike in Martin's name,
singing of the gifts won by persistent faith.
Who indeed could grasp these things in the mind? Who could paint them in song?
Who could count them, who set them forth? All talent
is defeated; the praises hold back tongues, overwhelmed.
Yet, though unequal to the glorious deeds that glory adorns,
which I have so often learned or read again in writing,
since I cannot speak as is fitting, I will at least strive to touch them.
A certain man, returning to his own threshold from the holy church,
believing he was bringing to his house a safeguard of salvation,
had carried with him to his home some holy wax,
trusting that the blessing of so great a patron joined to it
would, by the merit of so just a faith, be present with its power.
And now the time had come for proofs of the favour to be shown.
By chance, through a fire that had escaped, creeping rather unchecked,
the devouring flame, increasing its strength on the fodder of wood,
was already pressing the house with ruin. On every side the heat
rolled up a heaving mass in a great whirlwind into the air.
It swallowed up dry things, snatching them, and licking whatever was in its way,
and leaving only ashes from so great a disaster.
Nor was there hope of escape, as the danger blazed closer.
Terror, pressing on, had hemmed in the inner rooms,
and the neighbouring dangers [had hemmed in] a prey so close at hand.
Prayers returned to the saint. With faithful clamour
he is called upon, and many voices repeat the holy name.
The master himself, the glowing lights of the kindled wax,
pouring out a gentle light from their blessed fat,
swiftly snatches up with trembling right hand to the inner rooms,
and, setting them blazing in the midst of the flames,
with the defence of fire drove back the pressing fire.
The raging whirlwind halted. At once the ravaging enemy
turned its back, and a spark put to flight the fury of the fire.
Not so, if the clouds had cast down all their storms,
could the tempests poured down from above have availed,
or, if competing crowds had seized the rivers,
could any springs, with their stream drained, have been able
to bestow this boon so swiftly as did true power.
The fire, trembling, flees the wax, its own food,
and nature, in concord, dreads the honeycombs that nourish it.
By its power [the wax] kills the flame which it feeds with its light,
fragrant with clear nectar, with the richness of its liquid.
Having dared to run through these things hastily in few words,
I, unlearned, have set them down to be read again by the faithful people.
Such great joys have strengthened my humble voice.
What you will complain is too little described, you will marvel at as deeds.
It is enough that, scorning the poem, you praise the proclamation:
that death has had no power, since life is openly proven.
The city of Tours rejoices forever in Martin as its bishop.
